- Primary pulmonary arterial hypertension (Group 1): idiopathic remodeling of the lung vessels.
- Sleep-disordered breathing: chronic nocturnal alveolar hypoventilation.
- Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (Group 4): clot burden that never cleared.

cards.t: Alveolar hypoxia and hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction
k: why does COPD cause pulmonary hypertension
q: why is alveolar hypoxia the most important driver of pulmonary hypertension
what is hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction
how does COPD raise pulmonary vascular resistance
cards.x:
Alveolar hypoxia, low oxygen in the air sacs, is the single most important driver of pulmonary hypertension in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). It works through a reflex that is helpful in a healthy lung and harmful in a diseased one.

In healthy lungs, hypoxia in one small area triggers a focused narrowing of the vessels there. Blood is shunted toward better-oxygenated areas, which improves the match between ventilation and perfusion.

In the COPD "Blue Bloater," every alveolus is hypoxic and hypercapnic (high in carbon dioxide). So every vessel narrows. Pulmonary vascular resistance climbs sharply, and the right ventricle faces a relentless rise in afterload, the pressure it must push against.

cards.t: Loss of the lung vascular bed and polycythemia
q: how does emphysema increase pulmonary vascular resistance
why does polycythemia worsen cor pulmonale
what is the structural cause of high pulmonary resistance
cards.x:
Narrowing from hypoxia is only half the story. The second engine behind high pulmonary resistance is structural: the vascular bed itself is destroyed, as in emphysema, interstitial lung disease and fibrosis, and pulmonary embolism. This resistance is anatomical, not just functional.

The total cross-sectional area of the lung's vascular bed shrinks severely. With fewer channels to carry the same blood flow, resistance rises.

Polycythemia compounds the problem. Chronic hypoxia drives the body to make more red cells, which increases blood viscosity, so the heart works even harder against a bed that is already obliterated.

cards.t: Acute versus chronic cor pulmonale (how the right ventricle copes)
q: what is the difference between acute and chronic cor pulmonale
why does the right ventricle fail quickly in massive pulmonary embolism
how does the right ventricle adapt to chronic pressure
cards.x:
The right ventricle is a thin-walled, high-compliance, low-pressure chamber, so it is very sensitive to sudden changes in afterload. How it fails depends on how fast the pressure rises.

- Acute (for example, massive pulmonary embolism): the pressure outpaces any adaptation. Wall tension rises instantly, causing sudden dilation, stretch and microinfarction. Time course is minutes to hours. Typical picture: severe sudden dyspnea, sweating, rapid pulse, pallor, syncope. The threat is decreased left ventricular filling and shock.
- Chronic (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, interstitial lung disease, pulmonary arterial hypertension): the pressure rises gradually over months to years, giving time for concentric hypertrophy, then late dilation. Typical picture: unproductive cough, progressive exertional dyspnea, the "Blue Bloater" look. The threat is progressive volume overload, hypoxemia and right heart failure.

cards.t: Acute cor pulmonale: the chain from clot to shock (ventricular interdependence)
q: why does massive pulmonary embolism cause low blood pressure
what is ventricular interdependence
how does a failing right ventricle affect the left ventricle
cards.x:
In acute cor pulmonale, the right ventricle failure spills over to the left ventricle because the two share a wall, the interventricular septum. Think of it as a chain:

1. Massive pulmonary obstruction spikes right ventricular wall tension.
2. The right ventricle dilates acutely under the sudden pressure.
3. The shared septum bows leftward into the left ventricle.
4. Left ventricular diastolic distensibility and filling drop drastically.
5. Left ventricular cardiac output plummets, causing systemic hypotension and cardiovascular collapse.

The signs of the crash: distended neck veins (blood backing up behind the right ventricle), a tricuspid regurgitation murmur (the valve ring is stretched), tachycardia and pallor.

cards.t: Signs of chronic cor pulmonale once the right ventricle decompensates
q: what are the signs of chronic cor pulmonale
why does right heart failure cause ascites and leg edema
what does an RV heave mean
cards.x:
In chronic cor pulmonale the thickened right ventricle works for a long time, then eventually decompensates. Its high diastolic pressures transmit backward into the systemic veins and sharply raise hydrostatic pressure there. That backlog explains the findings.

On the chest:
- Right ventricular heave, a lift felt along the left sternal border.
- A loud pulmonic second heart sound (P2), the pulmonic valve closing hard against high pressure.
- A systolic murmur of tricuspid regurgitation.

From the backed-up veins:
- Tender hepatomegaly, from congestion of the liver.
- Ascites, fluid in the peritoneal cavity.
- Dependent peripheral pitting edema.

cards.t: Cor pulmonale diagnostic funnel: sorting Groups 3, 4 and 1
k: chest x-ray then V/Q then right heart catheterization
peel off one group at each step
q: what is the order of tests for cor pulmonale
how do you separate lung disease, clots and primary vascular disease
what does each step of the pulmonary hypertension workup rule in
cards.x:
Evaluating pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale means systematically separating three causes. Each step peels off one group:

1. Chest X-ray and pulmonary function tests. Interstitial markings or hyperinflation, with an obstructive or restrictive pattern, point to parenchymal (lung tissue) disease, Group 3. If the findings are normal or non-diagnostic, go on.
2. A ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) scan or computed tomography (CT) pulmonary angiography. Segmental defects point to thromboembolic disease, Group 4. If there is no thromboembolism, go on.
3. Right heart catheterization and echocardiography. These confirm right ventricular strain and measure exact pressures. An elevated mean pulmonary artery pressure with a wedge pressure of 15 mmHg or less points to primary vascular disease, Group 1.

A different order is used when screening for pulmonary hypertension (echocardiography, then the V/Q scan, then catheterization). Neither is the only order.

cards.t: Pulmonary function tests and chest film in cor pulmonale
q: what do pulmonary function tests show in cor pulmonale
what does the chest film show in pulmonary hypertension
why can the lungs look clear in pulmonary hypertension
cards.x:
These tests assess the lungs side of the problem.

Pulmonary function tests sort the pattern, which is crucial for classifying Group 3 pulmonary hypertension:
- Obstructive (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease): a reduced ratio of FEV1 (forced expiratory volume in 1 second) to FVC (forced vital capacity).
- Restrictive (interstitial lung disease): a reduced total lung capacity.

On the chest film, look for flattened diaphragms (hyperinflation in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) and enlarged central pulmonary arteries (high pressure).

The trap: in pulmonary arterial hypertension or pulmonary embolism, the lung fields can look deceptively clear even though the vascular disease is severe and life-threatening.

cards.t: Electrocardiogram and echocardiogram findings in cor pulmonale
q: what does the electrocardiogram show in cor pulmonale
what does echocardiography show in right heart strain
how do you spot right ventricular hypertrophy on an electrocardiogram
cards.x:
Two tests look at the right heart directly.

The electrocardiogram (EKG):
- Peaked P waves mean right atrial enlargement.
- A tall R wave in V1 means right ventricular hypertrophy.
- In chronic cor pulmonale, look for severe right axis deviation.
- It is abnormal in 70% of acute pulmonary embolism cases.

Echocardiography evaluates right ventricular enlargement and estimates the pulmonary artery systolic pressure. Its visual hallmark of severe right heart pressure overload is septal flattening during systole, which deforms the left ventricle into a "D-shape."

cards.t: The D-shaped septum on echocardiography
k: right heart pressure overload on echo
q: what is the D-shaped septum
why does the left ventricle look like a D on echocardiography
what does septal flattening mean
cards.x:
The D-shape is the picture of a right ventricle under too much pressure. When the right ventricle is enlarged and pressure-loaded, it flattens the septum, the wall it shares with the left ventricle, during systole. A flattened wall on one side deforms the left ventricle into the shape of a letter D.

It is the visual hallmark of severe right heart pressure overload, so spotting it tells you the strain is on the right side of the heart. It fits with cor pulmonale from lung or pulmonary vascular disease.

cards.t: Treating cor pulmonale: root cause and oxygen
q: how is cor pulmonale treated
why is oxygen so important in COPD-related pulmonary hypertension
what treatment goes with each cause of cor pulmonale
cards.x:
The prime directive: you cannot fix cor pulmonale without addressing the underlying pulmonary problem.

"Oxygen is a drug." In Group 3 pulmonary hypertension (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, interstitial lung disease), continuous supplemental oxygen is paramount. It directly reverses alveolar hypoxic vasoconstriction and mechanically lowers pulmonary resistance.

Then match the treatment to the cause:
- Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: bronchodilators and aggressive treatment of underlying respiratory infections.
- Acute pulmonary embolism: thrombolytics and anticoagulation, with volume if the patient is hypotensive.
- Pulmonary arterial hypertension (Group 1): specialized targeted therapies, including phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors, endothelin receptor antagonists and prostacyclins.

cards.t: Diuretics in cor pulmonale: the preload tightrope
q: why must diuresis be careful in cor pulmonale
what happens if you diurese a failing right ventricle too hard
why is too little fluid dangerous in right heart failure
cards.x:
Fluid management in cor pulmonale is a tightrope in both directions.

- Too much fluid: hepatic congestion and severe edema. Diuretics (loop diuretics, spironolactone) treat this fluid retention and ease the liver congestion and peripheral edema.
- Too little fluid: the damaged right ventricle strictly depends on elevated filling pressure, called preload, to push blood past the high pulmonary resistance. Cut its preload too aggressively and the left ventricle is starved of blood, which causes a disastrous drop in systemic cardiac output.

So the answer is careful diuresis, never aggressive. Another danger is hypokalemia (low potassium), which can trigger lethal arrhythmias.

cards.t: The five groups of pulmonary hypertension
q: what are the five groups of pulmonary hypertension
which groups are pre-capillary and which are post-capillary
what causes each group of pulmonary hypertension
cards.x:
Pulmonary hypertension is sorted into five groups by mechanism. A quick way to hold them: Group 1 is arterial, Group 2 is left heart failure, Group 3 is lung disease, Group 4 is clots.

Pre-capillary:
- Group 1, pulmonary arterial hypertension: obliterative and proliferative vessel disease from idiopathic causes, connective tissue disease, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) or schistosomiasis.
- Group 3, lung disease and hypoxia: chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, interstitial lung disease, sleep apnea.
- Group 4, chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension: obstructive, from chronic thromboembolic occlusion.

Post-capillary:
- Group 2, left heart disease: a passive obstruction to pulmonary venous outflow, as in heart failure with reduced or preserved ejection fraction or mitral stenosis.

Drawn apart:
- Group 5, unclear or multifactorial: hematologic, systemic and metabolic disorders, such as sarcoidosis.

cards.t: How pressure overload destroys the right ventricle (three stages)
q: how does pulmonary hypertension lead to right heart failure
why does pulmonary hypertension cause exertional syncope
what happens to the right ventricle over time under high pressure
cards.x:
The right ventricle goes through three stages as pulmonary pressure stays high.

1. Compensatory hypertrophy: the wall thickens to overcome the rising pulmonary vascular resistance.
2. Dilation and failure: the Starling mechanism fails, and the chamber dilates as its end-diastolic volume increases.
3. Ventricular interdependence: the dilated, pressure-overloaded right ventricle bows the interventricular septum into the left ventricle.

The clinical consequence is the key point. The bowing septum mechanically impairs left ventricular filling in diastole. That reduces systemic cardiac output and causes exertional syncope, even though the left ventricle's contractility is normal.

cards.t: Symptoms of pulmonary hypertension by World Health Organization functional class
q: what are the symptoms of pulmonary hypertension
why is syncope an ominous sign in pulmonary hypertension
what does World Health Organization class IV mean
cards.x:
Symptoms follow the World Health Organization (WHO) functional class, which tracks how severe the disease is.

- Class I-II (early, mild): exertional dyspnea and fatigue. Often the only early symptom, and frequently dismissed or blamed on deconditioning.
- Class III (moderate): dizziness and lightheadedness, with marked limitation of physical activity.
- Class IV (severe): syncope or presyncope. This is ominous because it signals a fixed, low cardiac output that cannot rise with exertion. End-stage disease adds abdominal bloating, early satiety and edema, present even at rest.

cards.t: Physical exam findings in pulmonary hypertension: four places to look
q: what physical exam signs suggest pulmonary hypertension
what is hepatojugular reflux
what do you find in the neck, chest, liver and legs in pulmonary hypertension
cards.x:
The signs of venous congestion come from four places:

- The neck veins: elevated jugular venous pressure. Look for large "a" waves early on, or regurgitant "v" waves when the tricuspid valve leaks.
- The chest: a palpable parasternal lift (right ventricular heave), accentuated pulmonic valve closure (P2), and a right ventricular third heart sound (S3) gallop, which indicates right ventricular dysfunction.
- The liver: hepatojugular reflux. Sustained moderate pressure on the liver raises the jugular venous pressure by more than 1 cm, which correlates with elevated right-sided filling pressures.
- The legs: peripheral pitting edema, which can extend to the hips and sacrum in severe cases, and cool extremities from low cardiac output and peripheral vasoconstriction.

cards.t: Pulmonary hypertension versus left heart failure
q: how do you tell pulmonary hypertension from left heart failure
why are the lungs clear in pulmonary hypertension
what wedge pressure separates left heart failure from pulmonary hypertension
cards.x:
The two can feel alike, but three things separate them.

- Symptoms: left heart failure brings orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. Pulmonary hypertension brings abdominal bloating, early satiety, profound fatigue and exertional syncope.
- Lungs and chest X-ray: left heart failure gives bibasilar crackles, wheezing, Kerley B lines and pleural effusions. In pulmonary hypertension the lungs are typically clear to auscultation, and the film shows enlarged central pulmonary arteries with peripheral pruning (attenuation).
- Hemodynamics: left heart failure has an elevated pulmonary capillary wedge pressure, above 15 mmHg. The pulmonary hypertension of lung or vessel disease (pre-capillary) has a normal or low wedge pressure, 15 mmHg or less, with an elevated mean pulmonary arterial pressure. Group 2 pulmonary hypertension is the left heart failure side.

cards.t: S3 and S4 gallops (extra heart sounds)
q: what is an S3 gallop
what is the difference between an S3 and an S4
what does an S3 mean in heart failure or pulmonary hypertension
cards.x:
Gallops are extra heart sounds. A simple way to keep the two apart: the third heart sound (S3) is "a big floppy left ventricle," and the fourth (S4) is "a stiffened, filled ventricle."

The S3 gallop is the marker of an overloaded, failing ventricle, so it is part of the bedside picture of acute pulmonary edema. In pulmonary hypertension the S3 comes from the right ventricle, and it indicates right ventricular dysfunction. It sits with the other right-sided signs: a parasternal lift (right ventricular heave) and an accentuated pulmonic valve closure (P2).

cards.t: Testing for pulmonary hypertension: echo, V/Q scan, catheterization
k: echo screens right heart catheterization confirms
mandatory gold standard right heart catheterization
q: which test confirms pulmonary hypertension
what is the best initial test for pulmonary hypertension
why do we use right heart catheterization
cards.x:
Pulmonary hypertension is worked up in three steps, each with a job.

- Screening, echocardiography: the most useful initial test. It estimates right ventricular size, function and pulmonary pressures, and it is crucial for spotting left-sided valve or heart muscle disease that can mimic pulmonary hypertension.
- Differentiation, ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) scan: the essential test to exclude chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension.
- Confirmation, right heart catheterization: the test that confirms the diagnosis. It directly measures mean pulmonary artery pressure, wedge pressure and pulmonary vascular resistance to definitively confirm pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension.

The cor pulmonale funnel starts with a chest film and pulmonary function tests, so there are two orders in play. Neither is the one required order. Echocardiography is the most useful initial test.

cards.t: Why the V/Q scan matters in pulmonary hypertension
q: why not rely only on CT angiography in pulmonary hypertension
what does a high-probability V/Q mismatch mean for treatment
which test excludes chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension
cards.x:
The ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) scan is the essential test to exclude chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH), pulmonary hypertension caused by clots that never cleared.

The clinical pearl: do not rely solely on computed tomography (CT) angiography. A high-probability V/Q mismatch dictates a completely different surgical pathway, thromboendarterectomy. That is why CT angiography alone is not enough.

cards.t: The pulmonary hypertension risk table (low, middle, high)
k: right ventricular failure signs high risk
q: how is risk assessed in pulmonary hypertension
what makes pulmonary hypertension high risk
how do I remember the pulmonary hypertension risk table
cards.x:
The risk table has three columns and five rows, so learn the middle column and the others are better or worse.

- Signs of right ventricular failure: absent, absent, present.
- Progression: slow, moderate, rapid.
- Syncope: none, occasional, repeated.
- World Health Organization (WHO) functional class: I or II, III, IV.
- Six-minute walk distance: more than 440 meters, 165 to 440 meters, less than 165 meters.

The rule to remember: once signs of right ventricular failure appear, the patient is automatically at high risk. The worst column (rapid progression, repeated syncope, class IV, under 165 meters) is the high-risk one.

cards.t: The three drug pathways in pulmonary hypertension
q: what drug classes treat pulmonary hypertension
what do PDE5 inhibitors do in pulmonary hypertension
how do I remember the pulmonary hypertension drug names
cards.x:
Targeted pulmonary hypertension drugs work through three pathways. Each one works on the signals that constrict or relax the smooth muscle of the lung vessels.

1. Endothelin receptor antagonists (ambrisentan, bosentan, macitentan): block endothelin-1 from binding, which prevents potent vasoconstriction and smooth muscle proliferation.
2. Phosphodiesterase-5 (PDE-5) inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil, the drugs ending in "-afil"): prevent breakdown of cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP), which enhances the nitric oxide pathway and promotes smooth muscle relaxation.
3. Prostacyclins and prostacyclin receptor agonists (epoprostenol, treprostinil, iloprost, selexipag; the memory cue is "prost" in the name): raise intracellular cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP). They are the most potent class for vasodilation and anti-platelet aggregation, and they are essential for severe disease.

Know the phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors well; know the other two by class and example.

cards.t: Choosing pulmonary hypertension therapy: vasoreactivity and risk
q: how is pulmonary hypertension treatment chosen
who gets calcium channel blockers in pulmonary hypertension
what is the treatment for high-risk pulmonary hypertension
cards.x:
Treatment is chosen in two decisions.

Decision 1: is the patient vasoreactive? If yes, high-dose oral calcium channel blockers.

If no, go to risk stratification:
- Low or intermediate risk (World Health Organization class II or III): start oral combination therapy, for example an endothelin receptor antagonist plus a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor. Early combination therapy is superior to sequential monotherapy (adding one drug after another).
- High risk (class IV or rapid clinical decline): start continuous intravenous or subcutaneous parenteral prostanoids, for example epoprostenol.

The critical rule: no single variable determines therapy.

cards.t: Supportive care in pulmonary hypertension: fluids, oxygen, exercise, vaccines
q: what supportive care do pulmonary hypertension patients need
should pulmonary hypertension patients exercise
what oxygen level is the target in pulmonary hypertension
cards.x:
Alongside the targeted drugs, four basics apply.

- Fluid: careful diuresis is central to managing right ventricular volume overload. Intravenous loop diuretics produce venodilation before the diuresis. Avoid aggressive over-diuresis, which drops preload and can crash cardiac output.
- Oxygen: keep PaO2 (arterial oxygen pressure) above 60 mmHg. Hypoxia is a potent pulmonary vasoconstrictor, so supplemental oxygen is critical, especially during sleep or exertion.
- Exercise: avoid strict bedrest. Regular, steady aerobic exercise in a supervised rehabilitation program is safe, prevents muscle deconditioning and improves fatigue.
- Prevention: annual influenza and pneumococcal immunizations are mandatory to prevent acute respiratory decompensations.

cards.t: End-stage pulmonary hypertension: advance directives, resuscitation, transplant
q: why talk about advance directives early in pulmonary hypertension
what is the survival after resuscitation in pulmonary arterial hypertension
when is lung transplantation used in pulmonary hypertension
cards.x:
Advanced pulmonary hypertension carries a risk of sudden death, so planning is part of care.

- Advance directives: sudden death or lethal syncope can be the first sign of progression, so early palliative care discussions and advance directives are essential.
- Resuscitation: survival is only 6% at 90 days after cardiopulmonary resuscitation in pulmonary arterial hypertension. The hypertrophied, failed right ventricle rarely recovers from arrest.
- Transplant: for highly selected patients who are refractory to maximal medical therapy, or who have pulmonary veno-occlusive disease, lung transplantation remains the only definitive therapeutic option. Continuous intravenous support may serve as a bridge to transplant.

cards.t: How pulmonary edema forms: the Starling forces
q: what causes pulmonary edema
how do hydrostatic and oncotic pressure cause pulmonary edema
what are the Starling forces in the lung
cards.x:
Pulmonary edema is fluid flooding the air spaces of the lungs. Three things decide whether it happens:

- An outward force: raised capillary hydrostatic pressure (Pc). This is the engine of cardiogenic edema.
- An inward force: plasma oncotic pressure, the counter-balance that pulls fluid back in.
- The barrier: the semi-permeable capillary membrane, which is intact but overwhelmed in the pressure type.

Push out against pull in, across a membrane. Edema comes when the push wins, meaning the outward hydrostatic pressure exceeds the inward oncotic pressure, or when the membrane itself breaks.

cards.t: Cardiogenic versus noncardiogenic pulmonary edema (pump versus pipe)
q: what is the difference between cardiogenic and noncardiogenic pulmonary edema
how does wedge pressure separate the two kinds of pulmonary edema
what is the first question to ask in edema
cards.x:
The first question in any edema is: pipes, pumps, or filter? The differential diagnosis springs from the answer.

- Cardiogenic (the pump is failing): intact capillaries are subjected to extreme hydrostatic backup. The pulmonary capillary wedge pressure is above 18 to 20 mmHg.
- Noncardiogenic (the pipe is leaking): the capillary endothelium is shattered and leaks protein-rich fluid. The wedge pressure is 18 mmHg or less.

So the wedge pressure is the dividing line: a high one points to a pressure problem from the heart, and a normal or low one points to a permeability problem in the lung's own capillaries.

cards.t: Causes of cardiogenic and noncardiogenic pulmonary edema
q: what causes cardiogenic pulmonary edema
what causes noncardiogenic pulmonary edema
is acute respiratory distress syndrome cardiogenic
cards.x:
Cardiogenic causes (the pump):
- Systolic dysfunction: ischemic loss of functioning myocardium, as in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.
- Diastolic dysfunction: myocardial stiffening and aging, as in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction.
- Valvular lesions: chronic aortic or mitral regurgitation, or severe stenosis.

Noncardiogenic causes (the leaky pipe):
- Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS): severe inflammatory destruction of the capillaries.
- Sepsis: systemic vasodilation and endothelial leak.
- Toxins: inhaled chemical injury to the alveolar-capillary membrane.

The pattern is that the cardiogenic causes all strain the heart, while the noncardiogenic ones injure the capillary barrier itself.

cards.t: Two wedge-pressure cut-offs: 15 mmHg versus 18-20 mmHg
q: why are there two different wedge pressure cut-offs
what wedge pressure is cardiogenic pulmonary edema
what wedge pressure separates pre-capillary from left heart disease
cards.x:
Two different wedge-pressure cut-offs show up, and each answers its own question.

- Is it edema, and is it cardiogenic? Above 18 to 20 mmHg means cardiogenic edema. A wedge of 18 mmHg or less means noncardiogenic.
- Is it cor pulmonale or pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension? A wedge of 15 mmHg or less with a raised mean pulmonary artery pressure means pre-capillary disease or cor pulmonale. Above 15 means left heart failure.

A wedge above 15 but not above 18 is therefore "left heart" by one rule and "noncardiogenic" by the other. Learn each cut-off with its own question rather than trying to merge them.

cards.t: How pulmonary edema looks at the bedside
q: what are the signs of acute pulmonary edema
what does pink frothy sputum mean
why does a patient with pulmonary edema tripod
cards.x:
Think of a picture rather than a checklist.

- Acute dyspnea, diaphoresis and tripoding: the catecholamine surge and the extreme work of breathing.
- Bilateral rales (crackles) and wheezing: the acoustic signature of fluid-filled airways and peribronchial cuffing.
- A third heart sound (S3) gallop: the marker of an overloaded, failing ventricle.
- Pink, frothy sputum: visual proof of a profound alveolar fluid shift and microvascular hemorrhage. It is a late sign.

cards.t: Tests for pulmonary edema: natriuretic peptide, echocardiography, catheter
q: what test shows pulmonary edema is cardiac
what does a high BNP mean in pulmonary edema
when do you need a pulmonary artery catheter
cards.x:
Three tests move the diagnosis along.

- B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) or N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP): proves ventricular stretch and volume overload. A substantial elevation separates cardiogenic dyspnea from pulmonary mimics.
- Transthoracic echocardiography: the best test for structural assessment. It defines left and right ventricular size, left ventricular ejection fraction and valve integrity.
- Pulmonary artery catheter or right heart catheterization: the ultimate hemodynamic arbiter. It directly measures left-sided filling pressures when the cause remains uncertain.

cards.t: Chest film signs of pulmonary edema (the wet-lung film)
q: what does pulmonary edema look like on chest X-ray
what are Kerley B lines
what is a batwing pattern
cards.x:
The wet-lung film has four descriptions to know:

- Batwing opacities: haze around both hila, the central perihilar distribution of alveolar edema.
- Peribronchial cuffing: edema thickens the walls of the bronchioles and causes characteristic blurring.
- Kerley B lines: short horizontal lines at the lung edge, from fluid engorgement of the interlobular septa.
- Bilateral pleural effusions: blunted bases, from fluid escaping the visceral pleura under extreme hydrostatic pressure.

Together they tell you the lungs are waterlogged from high pressure.

cards.t: Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure: what it measures
q: what is pulmonary capillary wedge pressure
how is wedge pressure measured
what wedge pressure confirms cardiogenic pulmonary edema
cards.x:
Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) is how doctors measure the pressure behind the lungs. A catheter is wedged into place and its balloon inflated. That creates a static column of blood that "looks forward" through the pulmonary capillary bed, so the catheter reads left atrial pressure.

The diagnostic threshold: a wedge pressure above 18 to 20 mmHg confirms cardiogenic hydrostatic failure, meaning the pump is failing and the pressure is backing up into the lungs.

cards.t: Pulmonary edema versus its mimics: heart failure, pulmonary embolism, COPD
k: heart failure versus pulmonary embolism versus COPD
q: how do I tell heart failure from pulmonary embolism or COPD exacerbation
which dyspnea causes have a normal BNP
what does the chest film show in pulmonary embolism
cards.x:
Three causes of sudden breathlessness are separated by a few clues.

- Heart failure (cardiogenic edema): distinguished by a highly elevated BNP (B-type natriuretic peptide), echocardiogram abnormalities and Kerley B lines on the chest X-ray.
- Pulmonary embolism, the "blocked pipe": often clear lungs on the chest X-ray, a normal BNP initially, and either right ventricular strain or a pattern of deep S wave in lead I with Q wave and inverted T wave in lead III (S1Q3T3) on the electrocardiogram (EKG).
- Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease exacerbation, the "inflamed airway": wheezing or hyperinflation on the chest X-ray, hypercapnia, and usually a normal BNP.

A markedly high BNP points to the heart; in pulmonary embolism it is normal initially, and in a chronic obstructive pulmonary disease exacerbation it is usually normal.

cards.t: LMNOP: the acute pulmonary edema toolbox
k: loop diuretics morphine nitrates oxygen positive pressure
q: what does LMNOP stand for
how do you treat acute pulmonary edema
why is morphine used with caution in pulmonary edema
cards.x:
LMNOP (loop diuretics, morphine, nitrates, oxygen, positive airway pressure) is a toolbox for acute pulmonary edema, not a rigid checklist.

- L, loop diuretics (given intravenously): rapid volume reduction through aggressive diuresis (furosemide, bumetanide, torsemide).
- M, morphine: use with caution. Historically used for venodilation and anxiolysis, it carries a risk of respiratory depression, and current heart failure guidelines advise against routine use.
- N, nitrates (given intravenously): immediate preload and afterload reduction through potent venodilation.
- O, oxygen and upright positioning: better ventilation/perfusion matching, and gravity physically lowers venous return.
- P, positive airway pressure (noninvasive positive pressure ventilation): mechanical alveolar stenting and preload reduction.

cards.t: How noninvasive ventilation and nitrates rescue the flooded lung
q: how does positive pressure ventilation help pulmonary edema
how do nitrates help pulmonary edema
why do nitrates lower pressure in the lung capillaries
cards.x:
Two of the acute rescue steps in the toolbox of loop diuretics, morphine, nitrates, oxygen and positive airway pressure (LMNOP) work by moving fluid or volume away from the lungs.

Noninvasive positive pressure ventilation does more than add oxygen. Positive pressure mechanically stents open flooded alveoli, forces fluid back across the membrane, and decreases intrathoracic preload and afterload.

Nitrates give potent venodilation. They rapidly shift volume into the peripheral venous capacitance system, away from the lungs, which directly lowers the outward capillary hydrostatic pressure (Pc) there. Nitrates are described as giving immediate preload and afterload reduction, and in flash pulmonary edema they are used to rapidly reduce afterload.

cards.t: Quadruple therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
q: what is quadruple therapy for heart failure
how do you prevent recurrence after pulmonary edema
which heart failure drugs reduce mortality
cards.x:
After the acute rescue, long-term treatment moves from managing volume to reducing deaths. That means blocking harmful neurohormonal activation. "Quadruple therapy" gives the greatest mortality reduction in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF):

- ARNI (angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor; sacubitril-valsartan): vasodilation and natriuresis.
- Beta-blockers: halt sympathetic toxicity and remodeling.
- MRA (mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists).
- Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT-2) inhibitors: the newest class for mortality reduction.

cards.t: Heart failure stages A to D and when to refer
q: what are the stages of heart failure
when is a heart failure patient referred for advanced therapy
what is stage D heart failure
cards.x:
Heart failure is staged A through D.

- Stages A and B: at risk and pre-symptomatic. The focus is prevention and risk modification.
- Stage C: clinical heart failure, the domain of quadruple therapy.
- Stage D: marked symptoms at rest despite maximal medical therapy, with frequent hospitalizations. This is the break point.

Reaching stage D is the referral trigger. It mandates immediate evaluation for advanced therapies: heart transplant, mechanical circulatory support with a left ventricular assist device (LVAD) or palliative hospice care.

cards.t: Pulmonary edema in four phases: from capillary to chronic rebuilding
q: how do I tie pulmonary edema together
what is the sequence from Starling forces to treatment
what happens at each stage of cardiogenic pulmonary edema
cards.x:
The whole story of cardiogenic pulmonary edema fits into four phases.

1. Microscopic failure: the Starling forces are disrupted, and capillary hydrostatic pressure exceeds oncotic pressure.
2. Hemodynamic crisis: the wedge pressure is elevated (above 18 mmHg), which triggers alveolar flooding.
3. Acute rescue: the toolbox of loop diuretics, morphine, nitrates, oxygen and positive airway pressure (LMNOP) shifts volume out of the central circulation and stents the alveoli open.
4. Chronic rebuilding: quadruple therapy remodels the neurohormonal landscape to prevent recurrence.

In short: recognize the failure at the membrane, measure the pressure at the wedge, and build the rescue at the bedside.

cards.t: Flash pulmonary edema: triggers, recognition and emergency care
q: what is flash pulmonary edema
what triggers flash pulmonary edema
how is flash pulmonary edema treated
cards.x:
Flash pulmonary edema is the sudden, severe form of pulmonary edema, with fluid flooding the lungs fast.

Cardiac triggers: acute myocardial infarction, severe ischemia or severe hypertension. In chronic heart failure, exacerbations from nonadherence, excess salt or rapid arrhythmias. The wedge pressure is elevated. A normal wedge pressure points to a noncardiac cause instead (acute respiratory distress syndrome, high altitude, sepsis, toxins).

Recognition: severe dyspnea, cyanosis, diaphoresis and pink frothy sputum; diffuse rales, rhonchi and expiratory wheezing; a chest X-ray with butterfly-pattern edema and vascular blurring; elevated B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP), and hypoxemia.

Emergency care: sit the patient upright with the legs dangling over the bed, give oxygen or noninvasive ventilation, intravenous (IV) furosemide for immediate venodilation and diuresis, and IV nitrates to rapidly reduce afterload. Hold outpatient therapy during acute kidney injury, continue oral beta-blockers unless the patient is in shock, and use morphine cautiously because it risks severe reduction of ventilatory drive.

cards.t: Deep venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism: one continuum
q: is deep venous thrombosis the same as pulmonary embolism
what is venous thromboembolism
how severe can pulmonary embolism get
cards.x:
Deep venous thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE) are not two diseases. Together they make venous thromboembolism (VTE), and they are a continuum of the same disease process. A clot forms in a deep vein and can travel to the lungs.

The physiologic effects and clinical consequences vary widely, from asymptomatic disease all the way to hemodynamic collapse and death. So a quiet leg clot and a collapsing patient can be two points on the same line.

cards.t: Risk factors for pulmonary embolism (Virchow's triad)
q: what is Virchow's triad
what are the risk factors for pulmonary embolism
what if a patient has no known risk factor
cards.x:
Pulmonary embolism risk factors fall into the three drivers of Virchow's triad.

- Hypercoagulability (blood clots too easily): malignancy, estrogen therapy, pregnancy, genetic thrombophilias, sepsis.
- Venous stasis (blood moves too slowly): prolonged immobilization such as flights longer than 8 hours, bed rest, paralysis, and heart failure of New York Heart Association (NYHA) class III or IV.
- Endothelial injury (vessel wall damage): recent surgery, central venous catheters, pacemaker wires, and pelvic or lower limb trauma.

One caution: not finding a known predisposition should never talk you out of an objective evaluation when the presentation fits an embolism. You do not need 15 risk factors, just a couple of good ones.

cards.t: The three presentations of pulmonary embolism
k: pleuritic chest pain hemoptysis pulmonary infarction
q: how does pulmonary embolism present
what does pleuritic pain with hemoptysis mean in pulmonary embolism
what does syncope in pulmonary embolism suggest
cards.x:
Pulmonary embolism shows up in three recognizable ways.

- Isolated dyspnea: sudden onset over minutes to hours. It can occur at rest or only with exertion.
- Pleuritic pain and hemoptysis: this indicates a distal, pleural-based pulmonary infarction (a wedge of lung that lost its blood supply). It is often accompanied by a localized friction rub.
- Circulatory collapse: syncope, severe hypotension and obstructive shock. This indicates a massive, proximal occlusion.

The location of the blockage shapes the picture: a distal, pleural-based one causes pain and hemoptysis, while a massive, proximal occlusion causes collapse.

cards.t: The dyspnea trap: a quarter of pulmonary embolisms have no shortness of breath
q: can you have a pulmonary embolism without shortness of breath
how often is dyspnea missing in pulmonary embolism
what is the biggest pitfall in diagnosing pulmonary embolism
cards.x:
Do not rely on shortness of breath. Approximately 25% of patients with proven pulmonary embolism completely lack dyspnea. If the story fits an embolism but the patient is not short of breath, the diagnosis is still on the table.

This is the one point to take away if you take nothing else about pulmonary embolism. Remember it as "beware the 25% of patients without dyspnea."

cards.t: S1Q3T3 on the electrocardiogram
k: deep S wave in lead I
q: what is S1Q3T3
is S1Q3T3 sensitive for pulmonary embolism
what does S1Q3T3 mean on an electrocardiogram
cards.x:
A deep S wave in lead I, a Q wave in lead III and an inverted T wave in lead III (S1Q3T3) make up a classic electrocardiogram (EKG) pattern. Its three parts:

1. A deep S wave in lead I.
2. A Q wave in lead III.
3. An inverted T wave in lead III.

It suggests severe right ventricular strain, not purely pulmonary embolism. The pattern is highly specific but has low sensitivity. That means that if you see it, it is meaningful, but with low sensitivity many patients with an embolism will not show it, so a normal tracing does not rule an embolism out.

cards.t: Chest film signs in pulmonary embolism: Westermark, Hampton's hump, Palla
q: what chest X-ray signs suggest pulmonary embolism
what is Hampton's hump
what does the Westermark sign show
cards.x:
Most patients with pulmonary embolism have an abnormal but non-specific chest X-ray, with findings such as atelectasis or an effusion. Three classic signs are highly suggestive but infrequent:

- Westermark sign: focal peripheral oligemia, an area of decreased vascularity.
- Hampton's hump: a wedge-shaped, pleural-based opacity that indicates infarction.
- Palla sign: an enlarged right descending pulmonary artery.

Because the classic signs are infrequent, most films show only the non-specific findings.

cards.t: The diagnostic path for pulmonary embolism: Wells first
q: what is the diagnostic algorithm for pulmonary embolism
when do you skip the D-dimer
why does pre-test probability matter in pulmonary embolism
cards.x:
Modern pulmonary embolism diagnosis starts with a pre-test probability from a clinical score such as the Wells criteria, worked out independently of any test. That probability dictates which test to order and how to read the result.

The path:
- Score is 4 or less (embolism unlikely): apply the Pulmonary Embolism Rule-out Criteria (PERC). If all are met, stop. If any fails, get a D-dimer. A negative D-dimer rules it out; a positive one goes on to computed tomography (CT) pulmonary angiography.
- Score above 4 (embolism likely): bypass the D-dimer and go directly to CT pulmonary angiography, or to a ventilation/perfusion scan if contrast is contraindicated.
- A positive CT pulmonary angiogram or high-probability scan confirms the diagnosis. The next step is to assess hemodynamic stability and right ventricular strain.

cards.t: The Wells score for pulmonary embolism
q: how do you calculate the Wells score
what score makes pulmonary embolism likely
is estrogen on the Wells score
cards.x:
The Wells score is a quick bedside tool. Add up the points:

- 3.0: clinical signs and symptoms of deep venous thrombosis.
- 3.0: pulmonary embolism is the number one diagnosis (more likely than the alternatives).
- 1.5: heart rate above 100 beats per minute.
- 1.5: immobilization for more than 3 days, or surgery in the previous 4 weeks.
- 1.5: previous deep venous thrombosis or pulmonary embolism.
- 1.0: hemoptysis.
- 1.0: malignancy (on treatment, treated in the last 6 months, or palliative).

A score of 4 or less means embolism is unlikely, so a total of exactly 4 is still unlikely; above 4 means likely, so 4.5 is likely. Previous clot is listed in the lower-weight box but is worth the same 1.5 as heart rate and immobilization, so learn the points, not the box label. Estrogen use is a risk factor and a rule-out criterion, but it is not a Wells item.

cards.t: The PERC rule for ruling out pulmonary embolism
k: rule out pulmonary embolism without testing
q: what are the PERC criteria
when can I stop the pulmonary embolism workup
does estrogen use fail PERC
cards.x:
The Pulmonary Embolism Rule-out Criteria (PERC) are a rule-out tool for patients whose clinical suspicion is very low (under 15%), and every single item has to pass. If all are true, stop the workup.

All eight must be true:
- Age under 50.
- Heart rate under 100.
- Oxygen saturation above 94%.
- No hemoptysis.
- No exogenous estrogen.
- No prior venous thromboembolism.
- No surgery or trauma.
- No unilateral leg swelling.

One failed item sends the patient on to a D-dimer. Estrogen use fails the rule. PERC is used only when the Wells score says embolism is unlikely, and both are outpatient rule-out tools.

cards.t: D-dimer: when it helps and when it does not
q: what does a negative D-dimer mean
who should get a D-dimer for pulmonary embolism
why is D-dimer not useful in hospitalized patients
cards.x:
The D-dimer is the second gate in the rule-out sequence. It is for low or intermediate probability patients who fail the Pulmonary Embolism Rule-out Criteria (PERC).

It has high sensitivity but low specificity. That is why a negative enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) D-dimer safely excludes pulmonary embolism, while a positive result does not confirm embolism and sends you on to imaging.

The D-dimer is designed for outpatients. In hospitalized patients it has limited use because of universally high false-positive rates. And if the Wells score says embolism is likely, you bypass the D-dimer entirely and go straight to computed tomography (CT) pulmonary angiography.

cards.t: CT pulmonary angiography versus the ventilation/perfusion scan
k: contrast allergy renal dysfunction embolism imaging
q: which imaging test do I use for pulmonary embolism
when do you choose a V/Q scan instead of CT angiography
can a negative V/Q scan rule out pulmonary embolism
cards.x:
Computed tomography (CT) pulmonary angiography (CTPA) is the first-line imaging for almost all patients and the standard for pulmonary embolism. It uses multidetector CT with sub-millimeter resolution of small peripheral arteries in a single breath-hold. The limits: it needs intravenous iodinated contrast, involves radiation, and risks overdiagnosing clinically insignificant subsegmental embolism.

The ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) scan uses a gamma camera to look for multiple segmental-sized mismatched perfusion defects. Choose it for renal dysfunction, severe contrast allergy, or critically ill patients (by a portable bedside perfusion scan). Its weakness is that it is frequently non-diagnostic if there is underlying cardiopulmonary disease, such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or severe heart failure.

A completely negative V/Q scan excludes pulmonary embolism with the exact same certainty as a negative pulmonary angiogram.

cards.t: Echocardiography in pulmonary embolism: for stratification, not diagnosis
q: is echocardiography used to diagnose pulmonary embolism
what does echocardiography show in massive pulmonary embolism
how sensitive is echocardiography for pulmonary embolism
cards.x:
Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) has poor sensitivity, about 50%, for diagnosing acute pulmonary embolism, but extremely high specificity for right ventricular strain. So it is a tool for risk stratification, not primary diagnosis.

What it shows in a massive embolism follows a cascade: the right ventricle is suddenly pressure-overloaded, the septum bows into the left ventricle (the D-shaped septum), left ventricular end-diastolic volume falls, and reduced left ventricular filling means crashed cardiac output and circulatory collapse.

cards.t: Pulmonary embolism risk tiers: low, submassive and massive
k: know the one in the middle
q: how is pulmonary embolism risk stratified
what makes a pulmonary embolism submassive
what defines a massive pulmonary embolism
cards.x:
Pulmonary embolism is sorted into three tiers, and blood pressure decides the top one.

- Low risk: normotensive, no right ventricular dysfunction and negative cardiac biomarkers. Excellent prognosis, with standard anticoagulation.
- Submassive (intermediate risk): normotensive (systolic blood pressure above 90), but with right ventricular dysfunction on echocardiography or computed tomography (CT) pulmonary angiography, or myocardial necrosis (an elevated troponin or B-type natriuretic peptide). These patients are at high risk for sudden deterioration.
- Massive (high risk): sustained hypotension (systolic blood pressure under 90 for more than 15 minutes), pulselessness or profound bradycardia, which means circulatory collapse. Mortality is high, and immediate advanced intervention is needed.

The tier to know best is the middle one: normal blood pressure, but right ventricular strain or a raised troponin or natriuretic peptide.

cards.t: Anticoagulation in pulmonary embolism: start now, then the 3-month decision
k: how long to anticoagulate pulmonary embolism
q: how long is anticoagulation given after a pulmonary embolism
when do you start anticoagulation in pulmonary embolism
what is the difference between provoked and unprovoked pulmonary embolism
cards.x:
Everyone with pulmonary embolism is anticoagulated. Phase 1 begins immediately on confirmed diagnosis, or on high clinical suspicion while awaiting imaging. Deep venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism are managed with identical baseline pharmacological principles. The goal is to halt clot propagation and allow the body's own fibrinolysis to clear it.

Phase 2 is the 3-month decision point, which depends on the risk behind the clot:
- Transient or provoked risk (recent surgery, trauma, hospitalization, estrogen therapy): consider stopping anticoagulation after 3 months.
- Persistent or unprovoked risk (active malignancy, hypercoagulable states, or no identifiable risk factor): indefinite anticoagulation is favored to prevent recurrence.

cards.t: Thrombolysis versus thrombectomy in massive pulmonary embolism
q: when is thrombolysis used for pulmonary embolism
when do you use thrombectomy instead of thrombolysis
should submassive pulmonary embolism get thrombolysis
cards.x:
For a massive (hemodynamically unstable) pulmonary embolism, the clot has to go, and there are two routes.

- Thrombolysis: pharmacological clot dissolution, given systemically or by catheter. It is the treatment for massive pulmonary embolism.
- Thrombectomy: physical extraction or maceration of the thrombus, as mechanical thrombectomy or surgical embolectomy. It is reserved for massive embolism when thrombolytics have absolute contraindications (recent surgery, active bleeding) or when there is a right heart "clot in transit."

In submassive embolism, thrombolysis is highly controversial. It weighs the chance of rapid right ventricular recovery against the risk of major bleeding and intracranial hemorrhage. The more the risk of hemodynamic collapse, the more aggressive the intervention, balanced against catastrophic bleeding.

cards.t: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension after pulmonary embolism
q: how do you screen for chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension after a pulmonary embolism
what is the treatment for chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension
what raises the risk of chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension
cards.x:
Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) is the long tail of pulmonary embolism. Screen for persistent or worsening dyspnea after 3 months of anticoagulation.

- No dyspnea: decide the length of anticoagulation by the risk of recurrent venous thromboembolism.
- Persistent dyspnea: get a ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) scan. Normal perfusion goes back to the length decision. Abnormal perfusion calls for a transthoracic echo, right heart catheterization and a pulmonary angiogram, then referral to an expert center for chronic thromboembolic disease (CTED or CTEPH). Anticoagulation continues during the workup.

Risk factors: unprovoked embolism, a delay in diagnosis of more than 2 weeks, right ventricular dysfunction on the first computed tomography (CT) pulmonary angiogram, and recurrent embolism.

The optimal treatment is surgical: pulmonary thromboendarterectomy.

cards.t: Pulmonary embolism in five steps: suspect, calculate, locate, stratify, treat
q: how do I put the pulmonary embolism workup together
what are the steps from suspecting to treating pulmonary embolism
what is the summary of pulmonary embolism management
cards.x:
The whole pulmonary embolism approach fits in five steps.

1. Suspect: recognize Virchow's triad, beware the 25% of patients without dyspnea, and watch for a deep S wave in lead I with a Q wave and inverted T wave in lead III (S1Q3T3) on the electrocardiogram.
2. Calculate: apply the Wells score. If it is 4 or less, use the Pulmonary Embolism Rule-out Criteria (PERC) and the D-dimer to rule out. If it is above 4, go directly to imaging.
3. Locate: use computed tomography (CT) pulmonary angiography as the standard test, a ventilation/perfusion scan for renal failure or allergy, and echocardiography to identify the D-shaped septum (right ventricular strain).
4. Stratify: massive (obstructive shock), submassive (right ventricular strain or biomarkers) or low risk (stable).
5. Treat: anticoagulate everyone, thrombolyze or thrombectomize the unstable, and screen for chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) if dyspnea persists at 3 months.

cards.t: Heart failure in adults versus older adults: how hard to diurese
q: how does heart failure management differ in older adults
why is diuresis gentler in elderly patients
what happens if you over-diurese an older adult
cards.x:
Adults and older adults differ in what is driving the edema and how much room there is for error.

- Adults: the pathology is usually an ischemia-driven loss of pump function. There is higher physiological reserve, so aggressive diuresis is generally well tolerated to clear volume.
- Older adults: the pathology is age-related stiffening of the heart muscle, which shifts the pressure-volume loop upward and means higher end-diastolic pressure. There is extreme sensitivity to changes in preload, so the therapeutic margin is narrow.

Older adults therefore need gentle, precise diuresis. Over-diuresis causes precipitous hypotension, and under-diuresis causes recurrent "drowning" (repeated flooding of the lungs). Right ventricular failure is the exception to aggressive diuresis for anyone: careful diuresis only.

cards.t: Older adults: PERC cannot be passed and diastolic stiffness drives edema
k: preserved ejection fraction edema older adults
q: why can't an older patient pass PERC
what is the workup for pulmonary embolism in an older adult with a low Wells score
why is early pulmonary hypertension missed
cards.x:
A few recognition points differ by age.

- Pulmonary embolism: the Pulmonary Embolism Rule-out Criteria (PERC) apply only under age 50, since age under 50 is one of its eight items. An older patient cannot pass PERC, so a low Wells score goes to the D-dimer.
- Pulmonary hypertension: early exertional dyspnea and fatigue are often misattributed to deconditioning.
- Clot risks to remember: estrogen therapy and pregnancy.
- Edema: in older adults, diastolic stiffening (preserved ejection fraction) drives the pulmonary edema.

cards.t: Rehabilitation and patient education for pulmonary vascular disease
q: what should I teach patients with pulmonary hypertension
what education does a patient with pulmonary embolism need
what rehabilitation do these patients need
cards.x:
The same rehabilitation and education plan applies to adults and older adults.

- Pulmonary hypertension: avoid strict bedrest and use supervised, steady aerobic rehabilitation. Keep oxygen so that PaO2 stays above 60 mmHg, especially in sleep or exertion. Give annual influenza and pneumococcal vaccines.
- Pulmonary embolism: explain how long anticoagulation will last (provoked: consider stopping at 3 months; unprovoked: indefinite), and do the 3-month dyspnea check for chronic thromboembolic disease.

cards.t: When to refer or involve palliative care in pulmonary vascular disease
q: when should a patient be referred for transplant or palliative care
who needs advance directives in pulmonary hypertension
when is an expert center needed for chronic thromboembolic disease
cards.x:
Each condition has its own referral trigger.

- Pulmonary hypertension: early palliative care discussions and advance directives, since sudden death or lethal syncope may come first. Lung transplantation for refractory disease.
- After a high-probability ventilation/perfusion mismatch: the thromboendarterectomy pathway.
- Persistent dyspnea with abnormal perfusion after a pulmonary embolism: an expert center for chronic thromboembolic disease.
- Heart failure stage D: immediate evaluation for heart transplant, mechanical circulatory support (left ventricular assist device) or palliative hospice care.

cards.t: Pulmonary nodule found by chance (coin lesion)
q: what is a pulmonary nodule
what do I do with a lung nodule found by accident
is a lung nodule usually cancer
cards.x:
A pulmonary nodule is a small spot in the lung, usually found by accident when a chest X-ray or chest computed tomography (CT) scan is done for some other reason. A single nodule seen on a chest X-ray is sometimes called a coin lesion.

The first question is size. Generally a nodule smaller than 6 mm is not concerning unless the patient is at high risk for lung cancer, for example someone who has smoked heavily for decades. Most nodules turn out to be benign. The main examples are a granuloma (an inflammatory lump) and a hamartoma (a growth of connective tissue). But if the patient is at high risk for lung cancer, the nodule is screened and worked up to rule out cancer.

cards.t: Why lung cancer is caught late
k: why is lung cancer so deadly
q: why is lung cancer so deadly
why is lung cancer found so late
which symptoms should trigger a lung cancer workup
cards.x:
Lung cancer is so deadly largely because it stays quiet. Patients usually do not have symptoms until the disease is advanced or has already spread, so by the time symptoms appear the cancer is far along.

There is also a trap with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). A person with COPD already coughs and gets short of breath, so a new cancer can be written off as just another flare and be missed.

Symptoms that should call for a workup for possible lung cancer: a persistent cough, coughing up blood, trouble swallowing, wheezing or shortness of breath, and body-wide symptoms such as weight loss, fever or fatigue, bone or chest pain, and endocrine disorders.

cards.t: Workup of a new solid nodule by probability of cancer
q: how do you work up a solid lung nodule
what happens if the chance of cancer is high or low
when is a lung nodule referred
cards.x:
For a new solid nodule of 8 to 30 mm, the first step is to estimate how likely it is to be cancer, using clinical judgment and/or a validated model such as the one developed by Mayo Clinic. That probability decides the next step. You do not need to memorize the exact percentages, just know that the nodule gets worked up.
- Very low (under 5%): computed tomography (CT) surveillance at 3 to 6, 9 to 12 and 18 to 24 months, using low-dose, thin-section, noncontrast scans.
- Low to moderate (5% to 65%): a positron emission tomography (PET) scan with a radioactive sugar tracer. Negative or mild uptake goes to the same surveillance. Moderate or intense uptake goes to a nonsurgical biopsy or video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery with resection.
- High (over 65%): standard stage evaluation, then video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery with resection if no metastases are found.

Referral to a pulmonologist, thoracic surgeon, interventional radiologist or oncologist is recommended for the high branch and for moderate or intense uptake.

cards.t: Benign versus concerning lung nodule features
q: what makes a lung nodule suspicious
what does spiculated mean
which nodule features are benign
cards.x:
A nodule gets your attention when it is bigger than 6 mm, sits in the upper lobes or hilar structures, has a spiculated appearance, is one of more than 3 nodules, keeps growing over time, enhances with contrast on computed tomography (CT), looks cavitated or nonsolid, or is in a patient at high risk of lung cancer. Spiculated just means spiky: spikes, deviations or lobulations in the border, like an angry star.

Reassuring features: well-defined borders, fatty tissue (a hamartoma), calcification in a benign pattern (see the calcification card), sitting close to a fissure (usually benign), and being smaller than 6 mm in a patient who is not high risk. Remember that most nodules are benign, either granulomas (inflammatory) or hamartomas (connective tissue growths).

cards.t: Calcification patterns in a lung nodule
q: which calcification patterns are benign
what does popcorn calcification mean in a lung nodule
which nodule calcification is malignant
cards.x:
The pattern of calcium (white) inside a nodule on imaging helps sort benign from malignant.

Benign patterns: diffuse (the whole nodule is white), central (a white core in the middle), popcorn (clustered rounded white blobs) and concentric (rings of calcium). Popcorn-looking calcification, or fatty tissue, points to a hamartoma, and a central calcification is typical of a healed granuloma.

Malignant patterns: ground-glass (fine specks scattered through the nodule, a stippled look) and eccentric (one off-center white fleck).

Quick way to keep them straight: calcium that fills the nodule, sits in its middle, or forms rings or popcorn is benign, while scattered specks or a single off-center fleck is not.

cards.t: Lung cancer screening criteria (low-dose CT)
k: who gets screened for lung cancer
q: who should be screened for lung cancer
how often is lung cancer screening done
what test is used to screen for lung cancer
cards.x:
Lung cancer screening is for high-risk people who have no symptoms and no known nodule. The criteria:
- Age 55 to 80.
- At least a 30 pack-year smoking history (a measure of how much and how long someone has smoked).
- Currently smoking, or quit within the last 15 years.

They are screened every year with a low-dose chest computed tomography (CT) scan, which uses a lower radiation dose than a standard chest CT. Medicare covers screening only from age 55 to 77.

A 2021 guideline update uses ages 50 to 80 and 20 pack-years, but the numbers to learn here are 55 to 80 and 30 pack-years. Screening is not for people with symptoms. A patient with symptoms gets a diagnostic workup instead.

cards.t: Upside and downside of lung cancer screening
q: what are the benefits of lung cancer screening
what is the downside of low-dose CT screening
why does screening cause unnecessary biopsies
cards.x:
The upside of screening is early detection, which can lead to rapid intervention and a better prognosis. Lung cancer is often silent until it is advanced, so catching it before symptoms is the point.

The downside is a high rate of false positives: findings that turn out to be benign. Those patients still get an unnecessary workup, and the workup can carry its own complications, such as from a biopsy.

Low-dose computed tomography works for screening because lung tissue has high contrast resolution between air and lung nodules, so the lower radiation dose still shows nodules well.

cards.t: Fleischner guidelines for following lung nodules
q: what are the Fleischner guidelines
how are incidental lung nodules followed
do I need to memorize the Fleischner tables
cards.x:
The Fleischner Society guidelines (last updated 2017) tell you how to follow and image-track lung nodules found by chance. Most places that produce chest computed tomography (CT) reports publish the Fleischner table right in the report, so there is no need to memorize the tables.

The ideas worth keeping: a single nodule under 6 mm needs no routine follow-up in a low-risk patient, and in a high-risk patient a CT at 12 months is optional. With multiple nodules, use the most suspicious one to guide management, and the follow-up intervals may vary with size and risk. For multiple nodules of 6 to 8 mm in a high-risk patient, the follow-up is a CT at 3 to 6 months, then at 18 to 24 months.

Ground-glass and part-solid nodules have their own separate table.

cards.t: Workup of a suspicious nodule: imaging, biopsy and labs
q: how do you work up a suspicious lung nodule
what is the standard test for a lung nodule
is sputum cytology useful for lung cancer
cards.x:
A chest X-ray is not a good tool for working up a suspicious nodule. It may be the first thing to show the nodule, but otherwise it is used to rule out other problems.

The standard workup is a computed tomography (CT) scan with contrast of the chest and upper abdomen, followed by biopsy or interventional treatment. Biopsy is done by bronchoscopy, through the chest wall (transthoracic), or by thoracoscopy, depending on where the nodule is, and it can be CT guided. A positron emission tomography (PET) scan and genetic testing are also part of it.

Labs include a complete blood count with differential, a comprehensive metabolic panel with calcium, alkaline phosphatase, and pulmonary function tests. Sputum cytology is not sensitive, so it is usually not done, with one exception: squamous cell carcinoma.

cards.t: PET scan for a lung nodule
q: how does a PET scan work for a lung nodule
does a bright PET scan mean cancer
what does low uptake on PET mean
cards.x:
A positron emission tomography (PET) scan uses a radioactive sugar called fludeoxyglucose (FDG). Highly metabolic cells take up the sugar, so a nodule that glows more than the tissue around it may be malignant. Think of tumor tissue as hungry for sugar. Low or normal uptake in the nodule is a good sign.

The catch is that PET does not rule out inflammatory conditions, because inflammation can also take up the sugar. A nodule that lights up still needs tissue to confirm what it is.

PET is also the scan that looks at lymph node involvement when lung cancer is staged.

cards.t: Suspicious nodule: surgery versus radiotherapy by fitness
q: what if a patient with a suspicious nodule cannot have surgery
when is segmentectomy used
what is the nodule treatment algorithm
cards.x:
The split that matters is whether the patient is fit for surgery.

Patients fit for surgery go to resection: a lobectomy (removal of the whole lobe), or a smaller anatomical segmentectomy for those who are unfit for lobectomy. A biopsy under image guidance can come first, and if it confirms malignancy the resection follows. If the biopsy is negative but there is concern about a false negative, consider a repeat biopsy or going on to excision or non-surgical treatment.

Patients unfit for surgery go to radiotherapy or ablation: stereotactic ablative radiotherapy (SABR), radiofrequency ablation (RFA) or conventional radical radiotherapy. If an image-guided biopsy is possible and safe it comes first, and if it confirms malignancy they get one of those treatments. If a biopsy is not possible or not safe, they go straight to them.

cards.t: Lung cancer: how common, how deadly
q: how common is lung cancer
what is the survival rate of lung cancer
can young people get lung cancer
cards.x:
Lung cancer causes more than 30% of cancer deaths in males, the highest mortality of any cancer in men. In females it causes more than 25% of cancer deaths and is ranked second, after breast cancer (current US data rank it first in women as well).

Survival is poor: only 17 to 18% of patients in the US are alive five years after diagnosis, one of the lowest five-year survivals of any cancer, and it is even worse in the rest of the world.

There are more than 200,000 new cases a year in the US and 2 million worldwide. Most occur in people older than 50, but about 4% occur under age 40, so you can't take lung cancer off the differential entirely just because a patient is young.

cards.t: Lung cancer risk factors
q: what causes lung cancer
how much of lung cancer is from smoking
does smoking always cause lung cancer
cards.x:
Smoking is implicated in 85 to 90% of lung cancers, and second-hand smoke in about 20%. The packs per day and the years of smoking compound the risk (5 times, 10 times, 20 times, and so on).

Smoking is not always involved. Adenocarcinoma occurs without it, while squamous cell carcinoma has the strongest link to it (some other references rank small cell carcinoma highest).

Other risk factors: exposure to radiation (and radon), air pollution, environmental and chemical toxins, tuberculosis or human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection, genetics, diet, and alcohol intake.

cards.t: Types of lung cancer (small cell versus non-small cell)
q: what are the types of lung cancer
how common is each lung cancer type
what is the difference between small cell and non-small cell lung cancer
cards.x:
Lung carcinomas are malignancies of epithelial cells, and there are two main types.

Small cell lung carcinoma (also called oat cell) makes up 15 to 20% of lung cancers. Non-small cell lung carcinoma is split by how the cells look under the microscope into adenocarcinoma (the most common; the shares given run from 30 to 40%), squamous cell carcinoma (20 to 30%) and large cell carcinoma (9 to 10%).

There are also mixed and rare types: carcinoid tumors, bronchial gland carcinoma, sarcomatoid carcinoma and Pancoast tumors.

A growing tumor, typically the small cell type, can also cause paraneoplastic syndromes, which are effects of hormones or cytokines secreted by tumor tissue.

cards.t: Type I versus type II pneumocytes
q: what do type II pneumocytes do
which pneumocyte gives rise to adenocarcinoma
what is the difference between type I and type II pneumocytes
cards.x:
Pneumocytes are the cells lining the alveoli, and there are two kinds.

Type I pneumocytes are squamous and extremely thin. They cover about 95% of the alveolar surface and do the gas exchange.

Type II pneumocytes are granular and roughly cuboidal. They cover only about 5% of the surface (3 to 5% of surface area) but make up about 60% of the cells in the alveolar epithelium, so they are the more common cell. Their job is to secrete pulmonary surfactant.

Type II pneumocytes are the usual origin of adenocarcinoma.

cards.t: How lung cancer develops and spreads
q: how does lung cancer develop
where does lung cancer usually form
where does lung cancer spread to
cards.x:
Carcinogens (or other reasons for a genetic mutation) activate oncogenes in lung cells, and further mutations or loss of regulatory control switch off the tumor-suppressing genes. Atypical cells then multiply, starting locally and spreading. Atypical epithelial cells in the bronchial mucosa may grow into the bronchial lumen, along the mucosa, or into the bronchial wall and nearby lung tissue.

The steps run from a genetically altered cell to hyperplasia (it divides faster), dysplasia (the cells change form), in situ cancer (it stays in one place), a malignant tumor (it invades and enters blood and lymph), and then metastases.

Most tumors form a mass in or near the hilum, but some form in the periphery, which makes them harder to diagnose. They spread to regional lymph nodes and to distant organs such as the liver, brain and bone.

cards.t: How lung cancer presents, including metastatic disease
k: lung cancer metastasis to brain liver bone
q: what symptoms does metastatic lung cancer cause
how does lung cancer that spread to the brain present
can lung cancer first show up without lung symptoms
cards.x:
Lung cancer often has no respiratory symptoms at first, and a patient may come in with complaints from a metastasis instead.
- Brain: headaches, vision changes, nausea, vomiting, syncopal episodes, seizures. Raised intracranial pressure can cause papilledema, and a tumor near the midbrain or pons can cause cranial nerve problems.
- Liver: dull right upper quadrant pain, a firm-edged enlarged liver, lack of appetite, jaundice, hepatic failure.
- Bone (anywhere, including the spine): bone pain, fractures even without a fall (a cough can cause a spinal fracture), spinal cord compression.
- Adrenal glands: adrenal insufficiency, with fatigue, weight loss, dizziness, hypotension and electrolyte imbalances.

When the cancer does cause lung symptoms, they are a persistent cough, coughing up blood, trouble swallowing, wheezing or shortness of breath, and weight loss.

cards.t: Low sodium in lung cancer: adrenal insufficiency versus SIADH
q: how do I tell adrenal insufficiency from SIADH in lung cancer
why can lung cancer cause low sodium
what goes with low sodium and high potassium in lung cancer
cards.x:
Two different lung cancer problems can both give a low sodium, and the rest of the picture tells them apart.

Low sodium with high potassium, low blood pressure, fatigue and dizziness is adrenal insufficiency from a metastasis to the adrenal glands.

Low sodium with confusion, seizures, ataxia, low serum osmolality and no edema is the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH) from small cell lung cancer.

The first comes from a metastasis in the adrenal glands. The second comes from the lung tumor itself, as a paraneoplastic effect.

cards.t: TNM staging of lung cancer: the big picture
q: how is lung cancer staged
what does TNM stand for
what makes lung cancer automatically stage 3
cards.x:
Lung cancer is staged once the first computed tomography (CT) scan, positron emission tomography (PET) scan and biopsy results are back. CT shows location and size, PET looks at lymph node involvement, and biopsy classes the tumor type. Staging uses the classic tumor, node, metastasis (TNM) system: T for the primary tumor, N for lymph node involvement, and M for distant metastasis.

The big idea is that more spread means a worse stage: a bigger tumor, nodes further away, or spread to the other lung or beyond all push the stage up.

Two rules: N2 (same-side mediastinal or subcarinal nodes) or N3 (other-side or scalene or supraclavicular nodes) automatically makes the cancer stage 3, and all stage 1 to 3 tumors are M0 (no distant metastasis). Tx and Nx are used only if there is no information at all about T or N. Mx is not allowed, because symptoms and exam information are always available. These tables are the 8th edition of the system; the 2024 9th edition splits N2 and M1c.

cards.t: T categories: tumor size and invasion
q: what are the T categories in lung cancer
how does tumor size change the T stage
what makes a lung tumor T4
cards.x:
The T category describes the primary tumor by its size and by what it has invaded. Bigger tumor, higher T:
- T1 (the smallest): 3 cm or less, surrounded by lung or visceral pleura and not involving the main bronchus (T1a up to 1 cm, T1b more than 1 to 2 cm, T1c more than 2 to 3 cm).
- T2 (second level): more than 3 to 5 cm, or main bronchus involvement without the carina, visceral pleura invasion, or atelectasis or post-obstructive pneumonitis extending to the hilum.
- T3 (third level): more than 5 to 7 cm, or a tumor of any size involving the chest wall, pericardium or phrenic nerve, or satellite nodules in the same lobe.
- T4 (the largest or most invasive): more than 7 cm, or invasion of the mediastinum, diaphragm, heart, great vessels, recurrent laryngeal nerve, carina, trachea, esophagus or spine, or a separate tumor in a different lobe of the same lung.

T0 (no evidence of tumor) and Tis (carcinoma in situ) are the other T labels.

cards.t: N and M categories: nodes and distant spread
q: what are N1, N2 and N3 in lung cancer
what makes lung cancer M1
what is the difference between M1a, M1b and M1c
cards.x:
Nodes: the further away the nodes, the higher the N.
- N1 (nearest): same-side (ipsilateral) peribronchial and/or hilar nodes, and intrapulmonary nodes.
- N2 (further): same-side mediastinal and/or subcarinal nodes.
- N3 (furthest): other-side (contralateral) mediastinal or hilar nodes, or any scalene or supraclavicular nodes.

Metastasis: M1 (distant metastasis) means stage 4.
- M1a: a tumor in the other lung, a pleural or pericardial nodule, or a malignant effusion.
- M1b: a single extrathoracic metastasis, including a single non-regional lymph node.
- M1c: multiple extrathoracic metastases in one or more organs.

In stage terms, M1a or M1b is stage 4A (the other lung, the pleura or pericardium, fluid, or one site outside the chest) and M1c is stage 4B (multiple sites outside the chest).

cards.t: Lung cancer stage 1 and stage 2 groupings
q: what defines stage 1A lung cancer
what makes lung cancer stage 2B
how do nodes change a small tumor's stage
cards.x:
Stages 1 and 2 are built from tumor size, with no distant spread. Stage 0 is carcinoma in situ.
- 1A: no more than 3 cm, no lymph nodes involved.
- 1B: more than 3 cm but no more than 4 cm, no lymph nodes.
- 2A: more than 4 cm but no more than 5 cm, no lymph nodes. A 4.5 cm node-negative tumor fits exactly.
- 2B: more than 5 cm but no more than 7 cm with no nodes, or a tumor no more than 5 cm that has spread to the peribronchial, hilar or intrapulmonary nodes.

So a 2.8 cm tumor would be stage 1A without nodes, but an involved same-side hilar node (N1) moves it to stage 2B. Mediastinal nodes (N2) would have made it stage 3.

cards.t: Lung cancer stage 3 and stage 4 groupings
q: what is stage 3A lung cancer
what separates stage 3A from 3B and 3C
what is stage 4A versus 4B
cards.x:
Stage 3 is built from larger size, invasion of nearby structures, or lymph nodes further from the tumor, and nodes in the mediastinum (N2) or on the other side (N3) always make it stage 3.
- 3A: more than 7 cm with no nodes, or growth into structures such as the diaphragm, mediastinum or heart; or more than 5 cm with same-side peribronchial or hilar nodes; or no more than 5 cm with same-side mediastinal nodes (subcarinal included).
- 3B: more than 5 cm with mediastinal nodes on the tumor's side; or no more than 5 cm with nodes on the other side or in the supraclavicular or scalene area.
- 3C: more than 5 cm with nodes on the other side or supraclavicular or scalene nodes.

Stage 4 is spread, whatever the size. 4A is the other lung, the lining of the lung or heart with secondary nodules, fluid around the lungs or heart, or one site outside the chest. 4B is multiple sites outside the chest.

cards.t: Central versus peripheral lung cancers
q: which lung cancers are central
which lung cancers are peripheral
how do I remember where each lung cancer type grows
cards.x:
A classic pointer: small and squamous are central.
- Small cell: central, but usually already metastatic by the time of diagnosis.
- Squamous cell carcinoma: the central bronchi, and it can be diagnosed by sputum cytology.
- Adenocarcinoma: the periphery, and not amenable to early detection.
- Large cell carcinoma: the periphery, and not amenable to early detection.

Memory aid: the two S's (small and squamous) sit in the center, and the other two, adenocarcinoma and large cell, go to the edges. If you know one pair, you know the other.

Lung carcinomas can also be mixed types, such as adenosquamous or combined small cell lung carcinoma.

cards.t: Adenocarcinoma of the lung
q: what is lung adenocarcinoma
how does lung adenocarcinoma present
which lung cancer is common in nonsmokers
cards.x:
Adenocarcinoma is a non-small cell lung cancer and the most common lung cancer. It is frequently found in the mid-lung and periphery, and often in association with peripheral scars. Its first metastases go to the lymphatics before it spreads out of the lungs. It is described as noninvasive, minimally invasive or invasive.
