The usual patient is over 50 with a smoking history, but smoking is not always associated with it. A persistent cough and shortness of breath with no signs of infection can be the clue.

It tends to be found late: about two-thirds of patients present with advanced disease or metastasis, because most are asymptomatic at first. Respiratory symptoms come first (cough, shortness of breath, chest tightness or pain, coughing up blood, fatigue), and later bone pain, weight loss and paraneoplastic problems. On computed tomography (CT), look for a peripheral, spiculated nodule that may involve the pleura.

cards.t: Where lung adenocarcinoma starts, how it grows, and mucicarmine staining
q: where does lung adenocarcinoma come from
what is lepidic growth
what does the mucicarmine stain show
cards.x:
Lung adenocarcinoma usually starts in type II pneumocytes, beginning with atypical adenomatous hyperplasia (AAH). At first the tumor grows in situ. Then it either enlarges along the alveolar lining (called lepidic growth) or starts to invade the stroma (minimally invasive adenocarcinoma). As it grows it may invade the pleura and then blood vessels, or form its own blood supply (invasive adenocarcinoma).

Under the microscope, a mucicarmine stain shows mucin production, which is related to adenocarcinoma. A negative stain may point to a large cell carcinoma instead.

Memory aid: adeno means gland, and type II pneumocytes are the glandular cells that make surfactant.

cards.t: Large cell carcinoma of the lung
q: what is large cell lung carcinoma
why is large cell carcinoma a diagnosis of exclusion
where does large cell carcinoma spread
cards.x:
Large cell carcinoma is a non-small cell lung cancer that is a diagnosis of exclusion. It lacks specific genetic or histology markers. It is anaplastic, undifferentiated and pleomorphic (variable in appearance), which separates it from adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma. Its cells are about 3 times larger than baseline, and it is classed away from small cell carcinoma because the treatments differ.

It tends to form in the periphery and forms necrosis or hemorrhage more readily than the other non-small cell types. On chest computed tomography (CT) it appears as a large, cavitated peripheral mass, as opposed to the central squamous cell carcinoma, but you still have to wait for biopsy with histology.

It can metastasize to unusual places such as the small intestine and bowel, which is specific to large cell. It has no standardized treatment because it is so varied and rare.

Current classification has shrunk this category: tumors with adenocarcinoma or squamous markers are now reclassified as those types.

cards.t: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung
q: what is squamous cell lung carcinoma
how does squamous cell lung cancer present
which lung cancer can be found with sputum testing
cards.x:
Squamous cell carcinoma is the second most common lung cancer (20 to 30%) and has the strongest association with smoking (some other references rank small cell carcinoma as the most strongly smoking-linked type). It is central, often originating in the bronchus, with frequent cavitation and obstructive phenomena.

It is silent at first. Once the tumor obstructs the bronchus, cough, wheezing and coughing up blood become likely, and it can look like a chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) flare that never settles. If the obstruction is large enough, part of the lung no longer fills (atelectasis) and the risk of pneumonia rises.

It spreads by local invasion, causing later signs such as trouble swallowing and voice changes (it can reach the laryngeal nerves), and by lymphatic spread to the hilar nodes.

Unlike the other lung cancers, it can be caught with sputum cytology. A high calcium is the paraneoplastic syndrome particularly tied to it. Treatment is a combination of surgery, chemotherapy, immunotherapy and radiation.

cards.t: Non-small cell lung cancer treatment by stage
q: how is non-small cell lung cancer treated by stage
when is surgery done for lung cancer
do non-small cell cancers respond to chemo and radiation
cards.x:
For non-small cell lung cancer the stage drives the plan. Surgical resection depends on tumor size and lymph node involvement, and the patient must be able to tolerate the surgery (survive and recover). Chemotherapy and radiation are described as only an adjunct to surgery, or used at stage 4, because non-small cell cancers do not respond well to them.
- Stages 1 to 2: surgical resection (adjuvant therapy may follow).
- Stage 4: cisplatin-based chemotherapy, with surgical resection only for a solitary metastatic lesion with a resectable primary tumor.
- Stage 3: the sources describe it two ways, so there is no single fixed rule. One description says surgical resection is used up to stage 3B with chemotherapy and radiation only as an adjunct. The stage table instead lists chemoradiotherapy for stage 3A, with surgical resection in selected patients, and chemoradiotherapy for stage 3B.

Chemotherapy and immunotherapy can now also be targeted to specific markers based on genetics and proteins. As a primary care or emergency medicine physician assistant (PA), the job is to screen, figure out risk, and refer.

cards.t: Types of lung resection (wedge, segment, lobectomy, pneumonectomy)
q: what is the difference between a wedge resection and a lobectomy
what is a pneumonectomy
how much lung is removed in each resection
cards.x:
The surgical options differ by how much lung comes out. Surgery can be done open or by thoracoscopy.
- Wedge: a small portion of a lobe.
- Segment: a larger portion of a lobe.
- Lobectomy: an entire lobe.
- Pneumonectomy: the entire lung.

The choice is based on the size of the tumor and lymph node involvement, and the patient has to be able to tolerate the surgery.

cards.t: Molecular and genetic testing in non-small cell lung cancer
q: why is lung cancer tumor tissue tested for genes
what are EGFR, KRAS and ALK
how does genetic testing change lung cancer treatment
cards.x:
Molecular analysis and genomic testing of the tumor look for specific mutations and proteins, which helps the oncologist tailor the therapy. Genes named:
- TP53 (tumor protein 53): a tumor suppression gene that lets cancer grow if it is damaged or mutated.
- EGFR (epidermal growth factor receptor).
- KRAS (the Kirsten rat sarcoma gene): a protein that promotes cell growth and survival.
- ALK (anaplastic lymphoma kinase): a gene making a kinase that promotes cell growth and fuses into other genes.

In adenocarcinoma, KRAS accounts for about 30% of mutations, EGFR 15% and ALK 5%. These are only examples; you do not need drug-by-marker details.

For non-small cell cancer other than squamous cell, genetic markers guide which chemotherapy drugs are used, and protein markers guide immunotherapy.

cards.t: Immunotherapy and checkpoint inhibitors in lung cancer
q: how do checkpoint inhibitors work
what is PD-1 immunotherapy
which lung cancers get immunotherapy
cards.x:
Immunotherapy uses monoclonal antibodies (the -mab drugs) for some patients, depending on the markers of their cancer, how they respond to traditional treatments, or if they are not a surgical candidate (for example stage 4 or metastatic disease).

Checkpoint inhibitors such as nivolumab and pembrolizumab work on the programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) pathway. Tumor cells can bind the immune T cell and switch it off. The drug blocks that binding (anti-PD-1, or against its partner, programmed death-ligand 1), so the T cell stays active and attacks the tumor cells.

Marker-based immunotherapy is described for non-small cell cancer excluding squamous cell, in combination with or after a poor response to chemotherapy; the management list for squamous cell also names immunotherapy, so squamous cell is treated as its own case. It is also becoming an option in small cell, where nivolumab and atezolizumab are approved as adjuncts in some cases.

cards.t: Small cell (oat cell) lung carcinoma
q: what is small cell lung cancer
why is small cell lung cancer found late
what does small cell look like under the microscope
cards.x:
Small cell (oat cell) carcinoma makes up 15 to 20% of lung cancers. It is central and infiltrates the mucosa, so it develops insidiously: over 70% of patients are already metastatic (liver, bone, brain) when it is detected. Once the tumor is large enough to cause symptoms, it also has a high cavitation rate. It is associated with a lesion on the short arm of chromosome 3.

It can develop from amine precursor uptake and decarboxylation (APUD) cells, which secrete polypeptide hormones, so neuroendocrine paraneoplastic symptoms can occur.

Under the microscope it is a fragile tumor that is often crushed during biopsy, but you can still see the small size of the tumor cells, the lack of nucleoli, and a high nuclear-to-cytoplasm ratio.

It responds better to chemotherapy and radiation than the three non-small cell cancers. Immunotherapy is less effective because of its genetic variability, but is becoming an option.

cards.t: Limited versus extensive stage small cell lung cancer
q: what is limited stage small cell cancer
what is extensive stage small cell cancer
why does stage matter for small cell radiation
cards.x:
Small cell lung cancer is put into three categories based on whether it has metastasized.
- Limited stage: confined to one area, with only local lymph nodes involved.
- Extensive stage: spread away from the local area.
- Combined: different histological types mixed together, with non-small cell.

Stage matters for treatment. Small cell does better with chemotherapy and radiation than the other lung cancers, and radiation works best when the cancer is limited stage: if the cancer is pretty limited, you can radiate it effectively. The assessment also includes a brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan (preferred) or computed tomography (CT) with contrast, if prophylactic cranial irradiation is going to be given.

cards.t: Prophylactic cranial irradiation in small cell lung cancer
q: what is prophylactic cranial irradiation
when is PCI given in small cell lung cancer
why radiate the brain in small cell cancer
cards.x:
Prophylactic cranial irradiation (PCI) means radiating the brain just in case there is metastasis. It is used in small cell lung cancer because the chance of metastases is so high.

It is given after a complete or partial response to treatment. In limited stage disease it is given, and in extensive stage disease it is considered, with or without thoracic radiotherapy.

It is not recommended in patients with poor performance status or impaired neurocognitive function. When PCI is not given, surveillance includes a brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan (preferred) or computed tomography (CT) with contrast every 3 to 4 months during years 1 to 2, because brain MRI is more sensitive than CT for brain metastases. Smoking cessation is part of follow-up too.

cards.t: Radiotherapy: how it works and its acute and chronic effects
q: what are the side effects of radiation therapy
why does radiation cause less nausea than chemotherapy
what are the chronic effects of radiotherapy
cards.x:
Radiotherapy uses a linear accelerator that fires beams of photons or charged particles at the targeted area. Several beams cross at the tumor, which limits the radiation to the rest of the body.

Acute effects are local: skin, mucosa and tissue changes (redness and darker skin, with a risk of ulcers), inflammation and hair loss in the treated area. It is less systemic than chemotherapy, so nausea and vomiting are typically limited.

Chronic effects: pulmonary fibrosis and scarring of treated tissues; cardiovascular fibrosis and other damage to the heart muscle, resulting in coronary artery disease, valvular disease or cardiomyopathy; lymphedema and fluid retention from lymphatic damage (think axillary); and neuropathy.

cards.t: Lung carcinoid tumors and carcinoid syndrome
q: what is carcinoid syndrome
what are the symptoms of a bronchial carcinoid
what valve problems does carcinoid syndrome cause
cards.x:
Carcinoid tumors are among the mixed and rare lung cancers. For lung causes, carcinoid syndrome comes mainly from a bronchial carcinoid. The cancer cells release serotonin, which causes symptoms in several body systems:
- Skin: flushing and apparent cyanosis.
- Heart: thickening and stenosis of the pulmonic and tricuspid valves, and endocardial fibrosis.
- Lungs: cough, wheezing and dyspnea.
- Liver: hepatomegaly.
- Gut: diarrhea, cramps, nausea and vomiting.
- Elsewhere: retroperitoneal and pelvic fibrosis.

The quick picture to remember: flushing, right-sided valve thickening, wheezing, an enlarged liver and diarrhea.

cards.t: Paraneoplastic syndromes of lung cancer
q: what are paraneoplastic syndromes
which paraneoplastic syndromes go with lung cancer
why might lung cancer first show up as an endocrine problem
cards.x:
Paraneoplastic syndromes result from hormonal or cytokine effects secreted by tumor tissue, either the primary tumor or a metastasis. The tumor starts to look like a neuroendocrine problem rather than a lung problem, so a patient may be found to have lung cancer by accident while being worked up for the syndrome. Lung cancer can involve different systems:
- Endocrine: the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH), seen in small cell, and hypercalcemia, particularly in squamous cell.
- Neurological: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, or cerebellar degeneration or brain encephalitis (autoimmune).
- Dermatological: acanthosis nigricans or dermatomyositis.
- Hematological: listed as a system, with no example given.

cards.t: SIADH from small cell lung cancer
q: why does small cell lung cancer cause SIADH
what are the signs of SIADH in lung cancer
why is there no edema in SIADH
cards.x:
The syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH) is a paraneoplastic syndrome of small cell lung cancer. Neuroendocrine cells in the tumor make too much antidiuretic hormone (ADH, vasopressin), and the body holds on to too much water.

The result is hyponatremia (low sodium) and decreased serum osmolality, which cause confusion, seizures, ataxia and other neurological problems. There are no signs of peripheral or pulmonary edema, because it develops insidiously over time.

It can be how the cancer is found: a patient may arrive in the emergency department confused and seizing, and the workup reveals lung cancer.

cards.t: Hypercalcemia in squamous cell lung cancer
q: which lung cancer causes high calcium
why check calcium in lung cancer
what paraneoplastic syndrome goes with squamous cell
cards.x:
Hypercalcemia is an endocrine paraneoplastic syndrome of lung cancer, and it is particularly tied to squamous cell carcinoma. Squamous cell cancers can make the calcium high. Calcium is also part of the lung cancer lab workup (the comprehensive metabolic panel).

So a smoker with a central cavitating mass and a high calcium points to squamous cell. Compare small cell, whose classic paraneoplastic syndrome is the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH), with a low sodium.

cards.t: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome
q: what is Lambert-Eaton syndrome
why does Lambert-Eaton cause muscle weakness
where does Lambert-Eaton attack
cards.x:
Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome is a rare autoimmune neurological paraneoplastic syndrome of lung cancer. It causes progressive, debilitating muscle weakness, particularly in the legs.

The immune system attacks calcium channels on nerve endings, at the neuromuscular junction. With the calcium channels not working, the nerve cannot release acetylcholine (ACh), the chemical that sends messages between nerves and muscles. Without enough acetylcholine, the muscles cannot contract properly, which causes the weakness.

It is rare, with a yearly prevalence of only 3000 patients.

cards.t: Why small cell lung cancer causes paraneoplastic syndromes
k: paraneoplastic syndrome first sign of lung cancer
q: why does small cell cancer cause paraneoplastic syndromes
what is the link between neuroendocrine cells and small cell cancer
can a paraneoplastic syndrome be the first sign of lung cancer
cards.x:
Neuroendocrine cells line the bronchioles. If a tumor sits among them and starts acting like a neuroendocrine cell, it produces weird neuroendocrine symptoms. That is the root of the paraneoplastic syndromes, and why they are typically seen with the small cell type.

The classic example runs: small cell tumor, to neuroendocrine cells in the tumor, to excess antidiuretic hormone, to water retention, to hyponatremia and low serum osmolality, to confusion, seizures and ataxia, with no edema.

This matters because small cell is insidious (over 70% are metastatic before detection), so the paraneoplastic picture may be the first sign of the cancer.

Not every syndrome is small cell: hypercalcemia is particularly squamous cell, and carcinoid syndrome comes from a bronchial carcinoid.

cards.t: Which lung cancer goes with which paraneoplastic syndrome
q: which lung cancer causes SIADH
which lung cancer causes high calcium
how do I remember paraneoplastic syndromes by lung cancer type
cards.x:
Three lung tumors have a classic hormone-type syndrome. Small cell lung cancer goes with the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH), which lowers the sodium. Squamous cell carcinoma goes with hypercalcemia, a high calcium. A carcinoid tumor goes with carcinoid syndrome, driven by serotonin: flushing, diarrhea and wheezing.

A memory aid: small cell Secretes a sodium-lowering hormone; Squamous Spikes calcium.

Where the pattern breaks down: the neurologic and skin syndromes (Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, cerebellar degeneration, encephalitis, acanthosis nigricans, dermatomyositis) are not tied to one cell type.

cards.t: Lung cancer: primary care role, referral and key numbers
q: what is the primary care role in lung cancer
when should a lung nodule be referred
what do I tell a patient about lung cancer risk
cards.x:
In lung cancer, a primary care or emergency medicine physician assistant (PA) is not doing oncology. The job is to screen, figure out risk, and refer.

Refer to a pulmonologist, thoracic surgeon, interventional radiologist or oncologist when there is a high probability of malignancy, or moderate to intense uptake on positron emission tomography.

Education points: smoking drives 85 to 90% of cases, and the risk compounds with packs per day and years of smoking. Five-year survival is only 17 to 18% because symptoms come late. Screening's upside is earlier intervention, and its downside is false positives and unnecessary workups. Most cases occur over 50, but about 4% occur under 40, so keep it on the differential.

Treatment depends on fitness: resection if the patient can tolerate surgery (a smaller anatomical segmentectomy if unfit for lobectomy); if unfit for surgery, stereotactic ablative radiotherapy, radiofrequency ablation or conventional radical radiotherapy.

cards.t: The pleura: parietal versus visceral layers
q: what is the difference between parietal and visceral pleura
which pleural layer feels pain
what does the pleural cavity do
cards.x:
The pleura has two layers with a potential space between them. The parietal pleura is the outer layer: it lines the inner surface of the thoracic cavity, the diaphragm and the mediastinum. The visceral pleura sits on the lung itself and covers the whole lung surface, including between the lobes.
- Blood supply: parietal from the systemic circulation, visceral from the pulmonary circulation.
- Hydrostatic pressure: higher in the parietal pleura, lower in the visceral.
- Sensory nerves: the parietal pleura has intercostal and phrenic nerve fibers, while the visceral pleura has none.

The pleural cavity holds about 10 mL of fluid (2 teaspoons), a thin film of serous fluid that lubricates the layers and keeps the lung coupled to the chest wall. The dome of the parietal pleura, the cervical cupula, is the landmark used to size a pneumothorax.

cards.t: Normal pleural fluid and how it is made and removed
q: what is normal pleural fluid
where does pleural fluid come from
what is in normal pleural fluid
cards.x:
Normal pleural fluid is a clear ultrafiltrate of plasma. It comes mainly from capillaries in the parietal pleura and is removed through the parietal pleura's lymphatics. Fluid inflow equals fluid reabsorption, and both depend on the balance of hydrostatic and oncotic pressure differences.

Normal fluid is low in cells and protein:
- pH 7.60 to 7.64.
- Protein less than 1 to 2 g/dL.
- White blood cells under 1000, mostly macrophages.
- Glucose similar to plasma.
- Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) under 50% of plasma.

cards.t: Intrapleural pressure and why the lung stays inflated
q: why is intrapleural pressure negative
what keeps the lung inflated
how do chest wall and lung pull on each other
cards.x:
Pressure inside the pleural cavity is always negative, slightly below atmospheric pressure: about 756 mm Hg against 760 mm Hg in the atmosphere and the lungs at rest, which is the same as about minus 4 mm Hg. It rises and falls with inspiration and expiration.

That negative pressure creates suction that keeps the lungs inflated. The reason is a tug of war: the chest wall's inherent tendency is to expand, while the lungs' inherent tendency is to collapse (elastic recoil). Air flows from high pressure to low pressure, like diffusion, which is the basis of breathing mechanics.

cards.t: Pleurisy (pleuritic chest pain)
q: what is pleurisy
why does pleurisy hurt when I breathe
how is pleurisy treated
cards.x:
Pleurisy is inflammation of the parietal pleura. It is not a diagnosis but a symptom. The inflamed layers rub together and stimulate the pain fibers in the parietal pleura, causing pleuritic pain.

The pain is well localized, sharp or stabbing, over the chest wall, and is worse with deep breathing, coughing, movement or sneezing. Inflammation of the parietal pleura on the central diaphragm (supplied by the phrenic nerve) may cause pain in the same-side shoulder or neck.

Causes include idiopathic, trauma, infection, inflammatory disorders such as systemic lupus erythematosus and rheumatoid arthritis, pneumothorax, pulmonary embolism, malignancy, and drug reactions (methotrexate, amiodarone, hydralazine).

Treatment is to treat the underlying condition plus nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).

cards.t: Pleurisy exam: friction rub and conditions to rule out
q: how do I tell a pleural friction rub from a pericardial rub
what should I rule out in pleuritic chest pain
what are the exam findings in pleurisy
cards.x:
On exam, pleurisy gives tachypnea with limited chest wall expansion on the affected side. Palpation and percussion depend on the underlying condition. Auscultation may reveal a pleural friction rub, which can sound grating, scratching or creaking, and may be heard in both phases of respiration. The key trick: a pleural friction rub disappears when the patient holds their breath, which differentiates it from a pericardial friction rub.

Immediately consider the big scary causes of this kind of pain: myocardial infarction, pericarditis, aortic dissection, pneumonia, pneumothorax and pulmonary embolism. Other causes to consider are rib fracture, costochondritis (inflammation of costal cartilage), vertebral fracture, and nerve root pain from herpes zoster. Diagnostic testing depends on the underlying condition.

cards.t: Pneumothorax: definition and the four types
q: what is a pneumothorax
what are the types of pneumothorax
what is an iatrogenic pneumothorax
cards.x:
A pneumothorax is air in the pleural space, which causes partial or complete lung collapse. The symptoms depend on how much of the lung has collapsed. Air gets in one of two ways: through the chest wall (for example, trauma) or through the lung tissue and the visceral pleura.
- Primary spontaneous: no chest trauma and no underlying lung abnormality.
- Secondary spontaneous: no trauma, but an underlying lung abnormality such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD, the most common), pneumonia, bronchogenic carcinoma, mesothelioma, sarcoidosis, tuberculosis or cystic fibrosis.
- Traumatic: blunt or penetrating chest trauma.
- Iatrogenic: injury to the pleura from a medical intervention, such as thoracentesis, subclavian vein catheter placement, bronchoscopy or mechanical ventilation.

Memory aid: primary is a flat tire out of nowhere; secondary is a flat tire you can explain. Iatrogenic is like trauma, but somebody with a license did it to you.

cards.t: Primary versus secondary spontaneous pneumothorax (the Marfan trap)
q: is a tall thin young man's pneumothorax primary or secondary
does Marfan syndrome make a pneumothorax secondary
why is secondary pneumothorax more dangerous
cards.x:
Primary spontaneous pneumothorax classically hits tall, thin young males, 20 to 40 years old (male more than female). Smoking is a significant risk factor, and family history may matter (an inherited association?). These patients usually have good pulmonary reserve, so severe respiratory distress is not common.

Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax comes with an underlying lung problem: COPD (the most common, through rupture of apical blebs), lung malignancy (which may be the first symptom), cystic fibrosis, pneumonia or tuberculosis, interstitial lung disease such as sarcoidosis, or connective tissue disease such as Marfan syndrome. It is the more serious event, because the diminished pulmonary reserve can be life-threatening and needs more immediate intervention.

The classic trap: a tall, thin young man looks primary, but if he has Marfan syndrome (an underlying abnormality), it is secondary. Any listed lung disease makes it secondary.

cards.t: Blebs versus bullae and why spontaneous pneumothorax happens
q: what is the difference between a bleb and a bulla
what causes a spontaneous pneumothorax
where do blebs form
cards.x:
A spontaneous pneumothorax usually involves the lung apex and is caused by rupture of apical blebs or bullae. Both are air spaces under the visceral pleura (subpleural). The difference is size: a bleb is small, less than 1 cm, and a bulla (plural bullae) is larger, more than 1 cm.

So the air that fills the pleural space comes through the visceral pleura when one of these blisters pops. This is the usual mechanism of spontaneous pneumothorax, and in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) it is the rupture of apical blebs.

cards.t: Spontaneous pneumothorax: history and symptoms
q: what are the symptoms of a spontaneous pneumothorax
how does a pneumothorax usually start
what else could it be besides pneumothorax
cards.x:
A primary spontaneous pneumothorax often happens at rest and may happen during strenuous exercise. There may be a history of a previous pneumothorax, since recurrence is common. A small one may cause no symptoms or only fatigue. The classic picture is acute onset dyspnea with ipsilateral (same-side) acute pleuritic chest pain, a severe stabbing pain that gets worse with deep breathing. Cough is less common.

A secondary spontaneous pneumothorax has the same symptoms, but generally greater, because the patient has less pulmonary reserve. An infectious cause may add cough, fever, chills or fatigue.

The differential includes myocardial infarction, pulmonary embolism, dissecting aortic aneurysm, pericarditis, pleurisy, muscle strain and costochondritis.

cards.t: Pneumothorax physical exam findings
q: what are the exam findings of a pneumothorax
why is percussion hyperresonant in a pneumothorax
why are breath sounds absent in pneumothorax
cards.x:
The exam can range from mild tachycardia to life-threatening respiratory distress, depending on the size of the pneumothorax. On the affected side:
- Inspection: tachypnea and decreased chest excursion.
- Palpation: decreased or absent tactile fremitus, because pleural air impedes the transmission of vibrations from the larynx to the chest surface.
- Percussion: hyperresonance.
- Auscultation: tachycardia, diminished or absent breath sounds (poor transmission of sound) and decreased or absent voice sounds, because the air in the pleural space blocks sound.

Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax has the same exam findings.

cards.t: Pneumothorax imaging: chest radiograph first, CT is the gold standard
q: what is the best initial test for pneumothorax
what is the gold standard for pneumothorax
what does a pneumothorax look like on chest X-ray
cards.x:
Don't confuse the best initial test with the gold standard. The initial test is a standard upright chest radiograph; computed tomography (CT) is the gold standard.

The radiograph shows the diagnosis by demonstrating the visceral pleural line, the interface between lung and pleural air: a thin, sharp line, convex (curving outward) toward the chest wall, with no bronchovascular markings beyond the edge.

CT is the best modality for determining the presence, size and location of a pneumothorax, assesses underlying disease, and detects blebs and bullae, but it is impractical when time is critical. In a CT, bulla cysts show concave margins while pneumothorax lines are convex. Radiographic tension signs, mediastinal shift and diaphragmatic depression, signal life-threatening tension.

cards.t: Sizing a pneumothorax (small versus large)
q: how is pneumothorax size measured
what is a small versus large pneumothorax
what is the cutoff for a large pneumothorax
cards.x:
The American guideline the course uses sizes a pneumothorax by the apex-to-cupola distance: the distance from the top of the lung to the cupola, the dome of the parietal pleura. Under 3 cm is small and 3 cm or more is large. It is a simple number, which is the point.

The British guidelines measure something different: the interpleural distance at the level of the hilum. The treatment tables word the cutoff slightly differently (more than 3 cm, 3 cm or less), so a pneumothorax of exactly 3 cm is not a clean test case. Newer British guidance (2023) leans on symptoms and risk rather than size and allows conservative or ambulatory care for some large primary pneumothoraces.

Size matters because treatment depends on the size, the patient's symptoms, and whether it is a first or recurrent episode.

cards.t: Deep sulcus sign on a supine film
q: what is the deep sulcus sign
how do you see a pneumothorax on a supine film
why is the costophrenic angle dark and deep
cards.x: The deep sulcus sign is a pneumothorax clue on a film taken in the supine position (lying on the back). It shows as a dark, deep costophrenic angle, caused by pleural air collecting laterally (along the side). On an upright film the clue is the visceral pleural line instead; on a supine film, look for the lucency (dark area) in the costophrenic angle.

cards.t: Lung ultrasound for pneumothorax
q: how does ultrasound diagnose pneumothorax
what is absent lung sliding
can ultrasound measure pneumothorax size
cards.x:
Lung point-of-care ultrasound is becoming an indispensable bedside tool for rapid diagnosis of pneumothorax, taking under a minute, and it is especially helpful in the unstable patient (trauma, intensive care).

Normal: lung sliding is present at the bright pleural line. Pneumothorax: lung sliding is absent, from loss of the apposed pleural movement. On M-mode, the stratosphere sign (parallel horizontal lines) replaces the normal seashore pattern. The presence of B-lines rules out pneumothorax.

The limitation: ultrasound does not assess the size of the pneumothorax.

cards.t: Arterial blood gas in pneumothorax
q: when do you get an arterial blood gas in pneumothorax
what does the blood gas show in pneumothorax
cards.x:
An arterial blood gas is often unnecessary in pneumothorax. The indications are severe underlying lung disease, or persistent respiratory distress despite treatment (tachypnea, use of accessory muscles, oxygen saturation under 92%).

The result depends on ventilation status and the body's compensation, and usually reveals hypoxemia (low blood oxygen) and respiratory alkalosis.

cards.t: Pneumothorax treatment goals and the toolbox
q: what are the goals of pneumothorax treatment
what procedures treat a pneumothorax
what decides how a pneumothorax is treated
cards.x:
The goals of therapy are to evacuate the pleural space, close the leak, and prevent or reduce the risk of recurrence.

The choice depends on severity (size and symptoms), the patient's clinical status, the cause, any underlying lung disease, prior pneumothorax, the risk of recurrence, available options and clinician expertise.

The options, sometimes more than one in the same patient: catheter aspiration, a Heimlich valve, chest tube (thoracostomy tube) insertion, pleurodesis, and operative therapy (video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery or open thoracotomy). For now, the goal is to recognize the problem and know what the toolbox looks like.

cards.t: Catheter (needle) aspiration for pneumothorax
q: how is catheter aspiration done
where is catheter aspiration done for pneumothorax
when is catheter aspiration contraindicated
cards.x:
Catheter aspiration removes pleural air with sterile technique: a large-gauge needle attached to a catheter, with a 3-way stopcock attached to a large syringe. The site is on the side of the pneumothorax, in the 2nd intercostal space, over the 3rd rib, in the midclavicular line. If more than 2 liters are removed, consider a persistent air leak. Obtain a post-procedure chest X-ray.

Seven situations are listed with this procedure: traumatic pneumothorax, tension pneumothorax, hemodynamic instability, underlying pulmonary disease, recurrent pneumothorax, bilateral pneumothoraces and bleeding disorders. The list itself carries no label here. Elsewhere, catheter aspiration is stated to be contraindicated in traumatic pneumothorax, in tension pneumothorax, and when there is underlying pulmonary disease.

cards.t: Heimlich valve
q: what is a Heimlich valve
why use a Heimlich valve for pneumothorax
cards.x: A Heimlich valve is a one-way flutter valve: air can flow out from the patient's end but not back in. It is small and portable, which promotes ambulation. It attaches to a tube inserted in the chest and is open to the air or attached to a drainage bag.

cards.t: Chest tube (tube thoracostomy)
q: what is a chest tube used for
where is a chest tube placed
when is a chest tube indicated
cards.x:
A chest tube is a clear plastic tube, in various diameters, with a series of holes at the distal end. Chest tube thoracostomy means placing the tube to drain fluid or air from the pleural space. The indications are pneumothorax or pleural effusion.

The most common site is the fourth or fifth intercostal space in the midaxillary line. An anterior approach between the 2nd and 3rd intercostal space at the midclavicular line is less common and specific to pneumothorax. There are options, and the choice depends on the patient's body habitus.

The tube connects to a drainage unit (collection, water seal and suction control chambers); the specifics of the chambers and tube sizes are not worth worrying about at this point.

cards.t: Pleurodesis (mechanical and chemical)
q: what is pleurodesis
how does pleurodesis work
when is pleurodesis used
cards.x:
Pleurodesis obliterates the pleural space by inducing inflammation inside it. The irritant makes the two pleural layers stick together (adhesions). That helps keep the lung inflated in pneumothorax, and leaves no room for extra fluid to build up in pleural effusion.

Indications: preventing recurrent or treating resistant pneumothorax, and pleural effusion. The most common indication is malignant pleural effusion (breast or lung cancer in most cases).
- Mechanical: manual abrasion of the pleura, via surgical intervention.
- Chemical: instillation of a sclerosant (drugs or talc) into the pleural space, via chest tube or thoracoscopically.

cards.t: Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery versus open thoracotomy
q: when is surgery needed for pneumothorax
what is VATS
what is the difference between VATS and open thoracotomy
cards.x:
Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) is an endoscopic procedure through small incisions in the chest. It gives access for stapling or resection of blebs and for pleurodesis, and it has largely replaced open biopsy. Robotic approaches are increasing.

Indications: recurrent spontaneous pneumothorax, bilateral pneumothorax, failure of tube thoracostomy (the lung fails to expand or there is a persistent air leak), and secondary pneumothorax, because of its high recurrence rate and the greater consequences of recurrence. The risks are patient discomfort, general anesthesia, and greater cost.

VATS has supplanted open thoracotomy for pneumothorax, but open thoracotomy remains a valuable option for complicated cases. Its benefits are examining the lung for the leak site and lysing previous adhesions, while its drawbacks are the anesthesia risks, higher cost and significant discomfort.

cards.t: Stable versus unstable pneumothorax
q: how do you decide if a pneumothorax patient is stable
what makes a pneumothorax patient unstable
cards.x:
A pneumothorax patient is considered stable if all of these are true:
- Respiratory rate under 24 breaths per minute.
- Heart rate under 120 and over 60 beats per minute.
- Normal blood pressure.
- Room air oxygen saturation over 90%.
- Able to speak in whole sentences.

All other patients are considered unstable. Don't overthink it.

cards.t: Treating primary spontaneous pneumothorax by size and symptoms
q: how is a small primary pneumothorax treated
when does a primary pneumothorax need a chest tube
what treatment is used for recurrent pneumothorax
cards.x:
Treatment depends on size, symptoms, and whether it is a first or recurrent episode. A rule of thumb: small is small, large is large.
- Small (under 3 cm at the apex), no or minimal symptoms: observation, adequate analgesia, and 100% oxygen by non-rebreather mask (it speeds the resorption of air). Repeat the chest X-ray in 6 to 12 hours to make sure it hasn't expanded. If stable and asymptomatic, discharge with a repeat film in 24 to 48 hours.
- Small with significant dyspnea after analgesia: catheter aspiration, a Heimlich valve or a chest tube. A chest tube is indicated if observation fails (an enlarging pneumothorax, persistent tachypnea over 30 breaths per minute, or saturation under 90% on room air) or aspiration fails.
- Moderate or large (over 3 cm) with moderate or severe symptoms: chest tube insertion.
- Recurrent: video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery with pleurodesis.

One more treatment chart lists simple aspiration or a small-bore catheter for a symptomatic, large (over 25% lung collapse) pneumothorax, so the materials give the large symptomatic case both ways.

cards.t: Treating secondary spontaneous pneumothorax
q: how is a secondary spontaneous pneumothorax treated
why is secondary pneumothorax managed more aggressively
does a small secondary pneumothorax need admission
cards.x:
Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax is more life-threatening because of the lack of pulmonary reserve, so it is treated more aggressively. Most are treated with chest tube insertion.

If it is small (3 cm or less at the apex-to-cupola) and the patient has no or mild symptoms, observation is possible. A chest tube is placed for symptoms or a persistent air leak, and the patient is hospitalized for monitoring and supportive care.

Surgery is another option: video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery or thoracotomy, with bleb stapling and pleural abrasion (mechanical pleurodesis). If surgery is not an option, chemical pleurodesis can be done through the chest tube. Catheter aspiration is contraindicated when there is underlying pulmonary disease.

cards.t: Pneumothorax recurrence, air travel, diving and patient education
q: how likely is pneumothorax to recur
when can I fly after a pneumothorax
what should I tell a patient after a pneumothorax
cards.x:
Explain the condition to the patient. Recurrence approaches 50% within three years after a first spontaneous pneumothorax. One-third of primary cases recur within one to two years, the risk rises above 60% after a second episode, and over 75% of recurrences are on the original side. The best preventive procedure is video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery with pleurodesis.
- Stop tobacco: smoking increases recurrence risk up to 100-fold, and quitting lowers it.
- Delay air travel 7 to 14 days after resolution, and confirm with a chest X-ray.
- Avoid scuba diving, since high-pressure activities carry severe recurrence dangers.
- Hold positive pressure therapies during an active air leak.
- Follow up with chest X-rays to confirm complete re-expansion.

Get a surgical evaluation if an air leak lasts over 4 days. Pilots and divers need early surgical evaluation, and a family history of spontaneous pneumothorax calls for a genetics referral.

cards.t: Traumatic pneumothorax: closed versus open
q: what is a traumatic pneumothorax
what is the difference between open and closed pneumothorax
what is a sucking chest wound
cards.x:
A traumatic pneumothorax follows a penetrating (gunshot or stab) wound or blunt chest trauma (a rib fracture tearing the lung), cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) or mechanical ventilation. Ask the patient: have you had any trauma?
- Closed: no external wound. Air enters the pleural space from the lung because of broken ribs or internal injuries.
- Open: a direct wound in the chest wall that lets air enter the pleural space during inhalation, which can lead to a sucking chest wound.

Catheter aspiration is contraindicated, and a chest tube is used to drain the air. A tension pneumothorax is a life-threatening complication. Mechanical ventilation is filed here under traumatic pneumothorax but also under iatrogenic pneumothorax elsewhere, so either label can appear.

cards.t: Tension pneumothorax
q: what is a tension pneumothorax
what are the signs of a tension pneumothorax
how is a tension pneumothorax diagnosed and treated
cards.x:
Tension pneumothorax is a life-threatening complication in which air enters the pleural space but cannot escape: a one-way valve traps it. Air comes in with inspiration and cannot leave on expiration, so pressure builds and pushes the mediastinum toward the other side.

That shift lowers venous return to the heart and cardiac output. The result is severe ventilatory compromise, hypotension, tracheal deviation away from the collapsed lung, distended neck veins, and decreased or absent breath sounds on the affected side.

It is a clinical diagnosis. Time is critical, so you don't wait for an X-ray. An immediate chest tube is ideal; if one is not readily available, perform immediate needle decompression, followed by a moderate or large chest tube and admission. Catheter aspiration is contraindicated.

cards.t: Needle decompression: where to put the needle
q: where is needle decompression done
what is the site for needle thoracostomy
how do the needle and chest tube sites differ
cards.x:
Needle decompression, also called needle thoracostomy, is inserting a needle into the pleural space to decompress a tension pneumothorax. The typical site taught is on the side of the pneumothorax, in the 2nd intercostal space, over the 3rd rib, in the midclavicular line.

The site is the same as for catheter aspiration. A chest tube goes elsewhere: usually the 4th or 5th intercostal space in the midaxillary line (the most common site), though it can go between the 2nd and 3rd space at the midclavicular line for anterior access in pneumothorax.

Options exist, so consider the patient's body habitus. In a large patient the needle at the second or third space may not reach, so the 4th or 5th space may be used: it is the typical site, not the only site.

Current trauma guidance (Advanced Trauma Life Support, 10th edition, 2018) moves the adult site to the fourth or fifth intercostal space just anterior to the midaxillary line; the course teaches the second intercostal space, midclavicular line.

cards.t: Tension pneumothorax: which findings fit and which do not
q: what is most associated with a tension pneumothorax
does tension pneumothorax cause hypertension
is subcutaneous emphysema in the neck a sign of tension pneumothorax
cards.x:
The finding most associated with a tension pneumothorax is tracheal deviation away from the collapsed lung, because the trapped air pushes the mediastinum to the other side.

The other signs are hypotension (not hypertension), distended neck veins, decreased or absent breath sounds and severe ventilatory compromise. Bradycardia is not among the findings listed for tension pneumothorax.

Subcutaneous emphysema in the neck is the pneumomediastinum finding, and it is not among the findings listed for tension pneumothorax, so it is the wrong choice when asked what goes with tension.

cards.t: Hemothorax and hemopneumothorax
q: what is a hemothorax
how is hemothorax diagnosed and treated
when does a hemothorax need thoracotomy
cards.x:
A hemothorax is blood in the pleural space. Trauma is the most common cause (injury to the heart or vasculature, the lung, or the intercostal, pulmonary or internal thoracic arteries); other causes include neoplasms, thoracic surgery and invasive procedures, torn adhesions or ruptured bullae, and systemic problems such as aneurysms and coagulopathies.

The diagnostic cutoff: the pleural fluid hematocrit must exceed 50% of the peripheral blood hematocrit. Bloody fluid with a hematocrit under 50% is a hemorrhagic effusion. Hemothorax is strictly an exudative effusion. Bedside ultrasound detects pleural fluid rapidly.

Treatment is a chest tube, the essential first step, to evacuate and quantify the bleeding. If blood loss is over 200 mL/hr, go to thoracotomy; surgery is also used for persistent hemorrhage or shock. Trauma guidelines also use 1500 mL or more on tube insertion, or more than 200 mL per hour sustained over 2 to 4 hours, before thoracotomy.

With both air and blood (hemopneumothorax), the air above the fluid makes a straight line with no meniscus. Retained blood can lead to infection, empyema, fibrothorax and trapped lung.

cards.t: Pneumomediastinum and the Hamman crunch
q: what is pneumomediastinum
what is the Hamman crunch
how is pneumomediastinum treated
cards.x:
Pneumomediastinum is air collecting in the mediastinal tissues. It happens spontaneously or after procedures or trauma. The possible causes are excessive pressure inside the alveoli that ruptures alveoli bordering the mediastinum, esophageal perforation, or esophageal or bowel rupture with air dissecting up from the neck or abdomen.

History: it may follow a sudden rise in intrathoracic pressure, such as violent coughing, vomiting or inhalation drug abuse (Valsalva). Symptoms are nonspecific: pleuritic chest or neck pain, sore throat, dyspnea and cough.

Exam: palpable subcutaneous emphysema in the neck, and the Hamman crunch, a substernal crackling or crepitance heard with each heartbeat, because the heart is beating against air-filled tissue. Think snap, crackle and pop.

Treatment: assess and maintain the airway and treat the cause. Air is often gradually absorbed; oxygen may speed absorption. Avoid physical activity and give analgesics. If severe, consult cardiothoracic surgery emergently.

cards.t: How a pleural effusion forms (pipes, pumps or filters)
q: why do pleural effusions form
how does heart failure cause a pleural effusion
how does cirrhosis cause a pleural effusion
cards.x:
Normally fluid enters the pleural space from parietal pleura capillaries and leaves through parietal pleura lymphatics. An effusion forms when one of these goes wrong. Think pipes, pumps or filters.
- Pump: heart failure raises capillary hydrostatic pressure.
- Filter: hypoalbuminemia (from nephrotic syndrome or cirrhosis) lowers the oncotic pressure in the vessels.
- Diaphragm leak: in cirrhosis and peritoneal dialysis, peritoneal fluid crosses the diaphragm through microperforations.
- Pipes: inflammation, infection, malignancy and trauma raise capillary permeability or change the permeability of pleural membranes, so the pipes leak. Malignancy and trauma can also decrease lymphatic drainage or block the lymphatic vessels completely.

The pump, filter and diaphragm problems make transudates; the leaky pipe problems make exudates.

cards.t: Pleural effusion: common causes and risk factors
q: what are the most common causes of pleural effusion
how common is pleural effusion
which side is hepatic hydrothorax on
cards.x:
Pleural effusion affects over 1.5 million patients a year in the United States, and is present in up to 62% of critically ill intensive care patients. Up to 30% have multiple concurrent causes. Malignancy and congestive heart failure are the frequent flyers: heart failure is the leading cause (about 500,000 cases a year), then infection, malignancy, pulmonary embolism, viral illness, cirrhosis and post-cardiac surgery.

Specifics worth knowing:
- Heart failure: left atrial pressure drives 85% of bilateral effusions.
- Infection risk factors: diabetes, alcoholism, immunosuppression, poor dental hygiene.
- Malignant effusion occurs in 15% of cancer cases (hyperpermeability) and can occur years after the diagnosis.
- Hepatic hydrothorax: ascites crosses the diaphragm; 80% are right-sided.
- Nephrotic syndrome causes effusions when albumin falls below 2 g/dL.
- Drugs: amiodarone, methotrexate, beta blockers.

cards.t: Pleural effusion symptoms and clues to the cause
q: what symptoms does a pleural effusion cause
how do symptoms point to the cause of an effusion
can a small pleural effusion be silent
cards.x:
A small effusion can cause no symptoms. When present, the most common symptoms are dyspnea, a dry cough and chest pain, due to pleural irritation. The pain can be mild or severe, sharp or stabbing, worse with deep inspiration, localized to the chest wall or referred to the same-side shoulder or upper abdomen (from diaphragmatic irritation).

Extra symptoms point to the cause:
- Lower extremity edema, orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea: congestive heart failure.
- Fever, purulent sputum and pleuritic chest pain: pneumonia.
- Hemoptysis: malignancy.
- Fever, night sweats, hemoptysis and weight loss: tuberculosis.

History matters too: heart failure, liver disease, trauma, a history of cancer, and asbestos exposure.

cards.t: Pleural effusion physical exam (versus pneumothorax)
q: what are the exam findings of a pleural effusion
how is the exam different between effusion and pneumothorax
does a small effusion show on exam
cards.x:
Small effusions (under 300 mL) give no physical exam findings. With a larger one:
- Inspection: asymmetrical chest expansion; the trachea shifts away from the involved side if the effusion is over 1000 mL.
- Palpation: decreased tactile fremitus, because fluid obstructs the vibrations.
- Percussion: dullness over the fluid.
- Auscultation: diminished or absent breath sounds over the effusion, with bronchial breath sounds toward its top; voice sounds decreased to absent but possibly increased toward the top; and sometimes a pleural friction rub.

Compare pneumothorax: it also has decreased fremitus and diminished breath sounds, but percussion is hyperresonant rather than dull. Another contrast: an infiltrate is fluid in the alveoli, like a sponge; an effusion is fluid in the pleural space pushing the lung around.

cards.t: Imaging a pleural effusion
q: how much fluid blunts the costophrenic angle
what imaging is best for a pleural effusion
when is a decubitus film used
cards.x:
On an upright chest radiograph, about 75 mL of fluid blunts the posterior costophrenic angle (seen on the lateral view) and about 175 mL blunts the lateral costophrenic angle. Upright is preferred, since supine films underestimate fluid volume.

A lateral decubitus film, taken lying on the side with the effusion side down, shows small amounts of fluid layering against the dependent parietal pleura, but it is almost never performed where bedside ultrasonography is available. Ultrasound has replaced it, identifies septations and thickening, and guides thoracentesis. For the very first test the materials differ: the upright chest radiograph is listed first, while one chart calls thoracic point-of-care ultrasound the preferred initial imaging modality.

Contrast chest computed tomography (CT) gives great detail, can identify as little as 10 mL of fluid, helps characterize the fluid, and shows pneumonia, tumors or pulmonary embolus, plus pleural nodularity and mass lesions.

cards.t: Loculated pleural effusion
q: what is a loculated effusion
why does a loculated effusion not move with position
what causes loculations
cards.x:
Loculations are fluid-filled compartments within the pleural space. They occur when there are adhesions between the visceral and parietal pleurae, and are associated with conditions that cause pleural inflammation, for example empyema.

The key difference from a free-flowing effusion: free fluid layers out when the patient changes position, while loculated fluid is stuck in a pocket. Ultrasound can show the septations and loculations.

cards.t: Thoracentesis and what to send the fluid for
q: when is a diagnostic thoracentesis done
what tests are sent on pleural fluid
how much fluid is removed in diagnostic thoracentesis
cards.x:
Thoracentesis removes fluid from the pleural space. A diagnostic thoracentesis removes 50 to 100 mL so the fluid can be seen and analyzed, and is done when there is a new pleural effusion with no clinical cause. A therapeutic thoracentesis removes fluid to relieve symptoms.

Send the fluid for: protein, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), white blood cell count (total and differential), Gram stain, cytology (to detect malignant effusions) and microbiological culture. The results then feed into Light's criteria, which sorts the fluid into exudate or transudate.

cards.t: Pleural fluid appearance (clear, cloudy, purulent, bloody, milky, black)
q: what does cloudy pleural fluid mean
what does milky pleural fluid mean
what does bloody pleural fluid indicate
cards.x:
What the fluid looks like gives a clue:
- Clear or straw: usually a transudative effusion.
- Cloudy: an inflammatory exudative effusion.
- Purulent: empyema (infected pleural fluid).
- Bloody: hemothorax or malignancy.
- Milky white: chylothorax.
- Black: a rare fungal infection.

Appearance alone is not diagnostic, so always interpret it with laboratory analysis and clinical findings.

cards.t: Light's criteria: exudate versus transudate
q: what are Light's criteria
how do you tell an exudate from a transudate
how do you apply Light's criteria
cards.x:
Light's criteria separate an exudate from a transudate. An exudate has high protein, from increased vascular permeability due to inflammation (fluid, protein and cytokines leak out). A transudate has low protein, from higher hydrostatic pressure or lower oncotic pressure (fluid moves across the membrane).

The effusion is an exudate if it meets at least one of these:
- Pleural fluid protein divided by serum protein is over 0.5.
- Pleural fluid lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) divided by serum LDH is over 0.6.
- Pleural fluid LDH is over two-thirds of the upper limit of normal serum LDH.

It is a transudate only if all three are absent (protein ratio 0.5 or less, LDH ratio 0.6 or less, fluid LDH at or below two-thirds of the upper limit).

Example: pleural protein 4.0 and serum protein 6.0 give 0.67, over 0.5, so it is an exudate whatever the LDH shows, because one criterion is enough.

cards.t: Pleural fluid lab patterns and what they point to
q: what does high lymphocytes in pleural fluid mean
what does low glucose in pleural fluid mean
what does elevated adenosine deaminase suggest
cards.x:
A few lab patterns in pleural fluid point toward specific causes. This is reference material, not something to memorize in detail.
- High neutrophils: bacterial empyema.
- High lymphocytes: tuberculosis, sarcoidosis or lymphoma.
- High eosinophils: air or blood in the pleural space, or asbestos.
- Low glucose or low pH: a complicated parapneumonic effusion, empyema or rheumatoid arthritis.
- Elevated adenosine deaminase with lymphocytosis: tuberculous pleurisy.
- Elevated N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide: congestive heart failure (an effusion that gets misclassified as an exudate).
- Elevated triglycerides: chylothorax.

cards.t: Causes of exudative pleural effusions
q: what are the common causes of an exudative pleural effusion
what is the most common cause of exudative effusion
what cancers cause pleural effusion
cards.x:
Exudative effusions come from conditions that make the pleura leak. Pneumonia is the most common cause of an exudative effusion. Malignancy is the second most common, and 75% of malignant cases are caused by breast carcinoma, lung carcinoma and lymphoma. Tuberculosis is the leading cause worldwide.

Other associated disorders: viral, bacterial, fungal and parasitic infections, connective tissue disease, asbestosis, pancreatic disease and chylothorax. Empyema and hemothorax are exudative effusions too.

cards.t: Chylothorax
q: what is a chylothorax
what causes a chylothorax
how is a chylothorax treated
cards.x:
A chylothorax is lipid from chyle (lymph fluid) collecting in the pleural space after the thoracic duct is disrupted. The thoracic duct carries chyle up from the cisterna chyli, so when it is disrupted, chyle leaks into the pleural space.

The most common cause is trauma, for example thoracic surgery. Tumors in the mediastinum can also cause it. Thoracentesis shows milky fluid with elevated triglycerides. If there is no obvious trauma, get a lymphangiogram and a computed tomography (CT) scan to assess the mediastinum.

Treatment: a chest tube or intermittent thoracentesis, but avoid excessive drainage, because heavy chyle loss can hurt nutrition. Octreotide (which mimics somatostatin) slows gastrointestinal secretions and decreases chyle drainage. Cutting long-chain triglycerides from the diet also decreases drainage, because they are absorbed through the lymphatic system.

cards.t: Empyema and parapneumonic effusion
q: what is empyema
what is a parapneumonic effusion
how is empyema treated
cards.x:
Empyema is purulent fluid (pus) in the pleural space. The most common precursor is bacterial pneumonia with a parapneumonic effusion, a pleural effusion that forms next to a pneumonia. If microorganisms infect that pleural fluid, a complicated parapneumonic effusion or empyema can result.

Suspect it when pneumonia symptoms do not resolve with therapy. The diagnosis is purulent material on thoracentesis; imaging may show loculations and fibrin membranes. A retained hemothorax can also lead to empyema.

Prompt therapy is critical: drainage and antibiotics, treatment of the underlying disease, and analgesia for pleuritic pain.

cards.t: Causes of transudative pleural effusions
q: what causes a transudative pleural effusion
what is the most common cause of a transudate
what is the difference between exudate and transudate causes
cards.x:
A transudate is a low-protein effusion caused by increased hydrostatic pressure or reduced oncotic pressure, and by definition all of Light's criteria are absent. Congestive heart failure is the star cause, behind more than 90% of cases. Other associated disorders are cirrhosis with ascites, nephrotic syndrome and peritoneal dialysis.

Pulmonary embolism is the odd one out: one list of transudative causes includes it, while the chart of exudative causes also lists it, so the materials do not settle which kind of effusion it makes.

Quick contrast: for exudates, think pneumonia first, then malignancy (breast, lung, lymphoma), with tuberculosis the leading cause worldwide. For transudates, think congestive heart failure first.

cards.t: Treating a pleural effusion
q: how is a pleural effusion treated
when is an indwelling pleural catheter used
when is pleurodesis used for an effusion
cards.x:
Treatment starts with treating the underlying disorder. Options:
- Diuretics: the initial treatment for transudates from heart failure.
- Therapeutic thoracentesis: relieves acute dyspnea and shows whether the lung can expand.
- Chest tube placement.
- Chemical pleurodesis: obliterates the pleural space in patients with expandable lungs. It is often used for recurrent malignant pleural effusions (lung, breast, ovarian cancer) as palliative care.
- Indwelling tunneled pleural catheter: best for non-expandable lungs or rapidly recurring fluid. It is placed as an outpatient and drained at home through a one-way valve into a negative-pressure bottle, minimizing time in hospital for patients with short prognoses.

cards.t: Pleurodynia (Bornholm disease)
q: what is pleurodynia
what causes pleurodynia
how is pleurodynia treated
cards.x:
Pleurodynia is a viral myalgia (muscle pain), often caused by coxsackie B virus, an RNA enterovirus. It typically follows an upper respiratory or gastrointestinal infection. The virus targets the striated intercostal muscles, causing inflammation or necrosis, which leads to frequent elevations in serum creatine kinase.

It starts with acute fever and pleuritic pain in adults or abdominal pain in children, with paroxysms of severe, knife-like pain lasting 15 to 30 minutes, with sweating and tachypnea. The patient splints the chest during an attack, and the involved muscles are usually tender.

Creatine kinase is elevated, and the chest radiograph is usually normal (it rules out other causes of chest pain). Treatment is supportive: nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and heat on the affected muscles. Symptoms resolve but can come back a few days later. How long an attack lasts is given differently in different sources (2 to 4 days in one, 4 to 6 days in another), so no single duration is fixed. Memory aid: it's a dynia, it's an itis, treat with NSAIDs and heat.

cards.t: Pleurodynia: cause, spread, testing and prevention
q: how is pleurodynia spread
how is pleurodynia diagnosed
how can pleurodynia be prevented
cards.x:
Pleurodynia is mainly caused by coxsackievirus group B (several serotypes) and echoviruses. It peaks in summer and spreads by fecal-oral contamination and contaminated water.

Besides acute, sharp pleuritic chest pain, patients may have fever, headache, sore throat, malaise and nausea, with tenderness, hyperesthesia and swelling over the diaphragmatic muscles. Orchitis and aseptic meningitis occur in under 10%.

Routine labs show no characteristic abnormality (creatine kinase is the exception). Testing includes enterovirus RNA polymerase chain reaction, viral culture from throat washings or stool, and a rise in neutralizing antibodies in convalescence.

Management is supportive pain and fever care. The course is self-limited and benign, without long-term sequelae. Prevention is thorough hand hygiene plus pool chlorination and pH control.

cards.t: When pleural problems need surgical or specialty referral
k: when to refer pneumothorax to surgery
q: when should a pneumothorax go to surgery
when do pleural problems need referral
what is palliative care for pleural effusions
cards.x:
Several pleural problems have clear triggers for surgical or specialty help.
- Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery: for recurrence, bilateral pneumothorax, or failed tube thoracostomy; also for secondary pneumothorax, because of its high recurrence and greater consequences. For a secondary pneumothorax, if surgery is not an option, chemical pleurodesis can be done through a chest tube.
- Surgical evaluation: for a persistent air leak.
- Thoracotomy: for hemothorax bleeding over 200 mL/hr.
- Emergent cardiothoracic surgery: for severe pneumomediastinum.
- Palliative care: pleurodesis for recurrent malignant effusions (lung, breast, ovarian), or an indwelling tunneled catheter placed as an outpatient and drained at home for short prognoses or a non-expandable lung.
